Autonomous mobility service · Technical specification

0.3Diagram notation

Sequence diagrams

  • Solid arrow: request, command or event sent.
  • Dashed arrow: result, acknowledgement or returned state.
  • Band with accent edge: operator (alt, else, opt, loop, par, guard) and its condition in brackets; band with dark edge: named phase of the flow.
  • PDF figures number steps 01, 02 …; detail figures number steps 1, 2, ….

State machines and flows

  • Filled dot: initial state. Tinted box: target or terminal state of interest.
  • Transition label: triggering event, then the guard in brackets where stated.
  • Dashed connector: feedback, return or recovery path.
  • Diamond: decision; every outcome is labelled.

0.5Scope and document structure

This specification defines the proposed product, service and system design of a regional autonomous mobility service with integrated reservation, dispatch, energy coordination and remote operation. It covers the customer touchpoints and their measurement (Part 1), the common platform, its containers, interfaces, remote operation and capacity rules (Part 2), and their requirements, interfaces and open decisions (Appendices C–E). Vehicle-internal automated driving functions are outside its scope; the ADS retains the dynamic driving task and fallback (P14).

1.DDetailed specification

This section specifies the product outcome that the rest of the document is designed to test: who takes part in the service, which consented signals the product may use and under which conditions, how the five value mechanisms are expressed as use cases over the end-to-end service loop, which rules bind every mechanism, and how each mechanism is judged. It defines the product-level contract that Part 2 (P08–P30) implements; it does not restate component internals, which are specified in the chapters referenced below.

1.D.1 Purpose and scope

The product hypothesis is deliberately narrow: customer intent and shared transport capacity can improve service outcomes, and that improvement can be decomposed into five mechanisms that are tested separately and then together. The chapter therefore fixes three things that later chapters must not change: the participants and what each controls, the information the product is allowed to act on, and the service contract that keeps passenger, shipment and cost records separate when capacity is shared.

In scope are the four participant roles, the consented signals, the MaaS product layer as a chain of responsibilities across C01–C07, the five-stage service loop, the five value mechanisms and the service contract and value test. Out of scope here are the internal design of booking, reservation, dispatch, energy and settlement (P08–P12), remote operation, roadside sensing and operator workflows (P13–P23), capacity and continuity (P25–P28) and the detailed sharing rules (P29–P30). Where this section names a behaviour that one of those chapters specifies, it links to it rather than redefining it.

The whole chapter is a proposed concept: the mechanisms are hypotheses to be validated through the experiment and gate process of P06–P07 (ASM-001, ASM-029). Nothing in this section asserts that any mechanism produces a gain.

1.D.2 Users and scenarios

The service is used by people with an intended arrival and a timing constraint, not by people who simply hail a vehicle. The scenarios below describe the user problems each mechanism addresses. They are illustrative of the hypothesis and carry no claim about frequency or size.

Planned arrival
A resident has a fixed appointment and books ahead. The problem is uncertain wait at pickup and, for the operator, empty travel to reach the pickup point. The received plan and its lead time are the information that mechanism 01 uses to position reachable supply before pickup.
Free time at a destination
A visitor has an interval between two commitments and has opted in to suggestions. The problem is that neither the visitor nor the provider knows that a feasible activity and trip fit that interval. Mechanism 02 offers such a combination only when spare capacity exists and the combined plan is feasible.
Flexible timing
A resident has a window within which the trip may move and is willing to move for a different total price. The operator's problem is peak load and missed pickups. Mechanism 03 offers a time shift with the alternative total price; the original booking remains valid if the offer is declined.
Compatible journeys
Two parties travel along overlapping routes. Each accepts sharing only within its own seat, access and detour limits. Mechanism 04 matches them only when every accepted limit still holds after insertion.
Eligible cargo on a passenger route
A provider has a shipment whose route overlaps passenger journeys. The problem is spare payload and space on passenger missions. Mechanism 05 inserts the shipment only within payload, space, handling and time limits and only when no passenger commitment is broken.
Underserved place or user
The city partner's problem is not a single journey but coverage: whether outcomes for underserved places and users are visible and reviewed. This is a reporting requirement on the measurement contract, not an additional mechanism.

Each scenario contains a failure that the design must handle as a first-class outcome: a cancellation after positioning, a refused or expired offer, a declined shift, a sharing match that breaks a limit, a failed cargo handover. Evaluation includes these outcomes rather than filtering them out: pilot exit evidence covers rejected, cancelled and recovered journeys (SVC-028), offer measures retain refusals and expired offers (SVC-055), and a gain is recorded as failed when any accepted service limit breaks (SVC-059).

1.D.3 Actors and responsibilities

The four participant roles each contribute information or capacity, and each retains a form of control that the product must not take away. The table states what each role supplies, what it receives, what it retains and where its obligations are specified.

RoleSuppliesReceivesRetainsSpecified in
Resident / visitorPlans, free time and preferences, each under consentFeasible offers with timing, total price and cancellation terms; live status; outcome and refund statusControl of timing, price and accessibility needs; the right to decline and keep the original plan; consent withdrawalP04; SVC-005; SVC-035
Mobility operatorReachable vehicles, finite operating capacity, exception handlingReceived plans, committed trips, cases with owner and deadlineOwnership of exceptions; protection of committed trips; the decision not to promise when capacity is absentP04 Operator workspace; P21; SVC-042
Service providerActivity slots, prices and service capacity; confirmations and observed useReservations and their changesService responsibility, staffing and handover obligations for its activityP23 16.1; TBD-039
City partnerODD, access and coverage conditionsOutcome reports, including underserved places and usersSetting of the conditions under which the service may operateP03 G2 constraint register; TBD-011

Within the product, responsibility is assigned per component along the MaaS product layer, and each entity has exactly one writing component (PLT-009). C01 admits requests and enforces identity, tenant access, consent and schema; C02 owns booking intent, consent records and the customer and provider outcomes; C03 decides feasibility and holds capacity; C04 executes and observes missions; C06 owns support cases and recovery; C07 owns usage and settlement. C05 is not a stage in the chain: it constrains which supply C03 may treat as feasible (SVC-015). The ownership table and the end-to-end sequence are in D01.1 and D01.2; the container views are in Appendix B.

1.D.4 Consented signals: data and handling

The product may act on four kinds of signal. Each is useful only if it arrives before the decision it informs, and each is personal information about a person's plans. The design therefore treats every signal as a record with a purpose, an expiry and a withdrawal path, recorded at the time it is received (SVC-001, SVC-002).

SignalMechanisms that use itDecision it informsHandling rule
Intended arrival01, 04, 05Positioning of reachable supply; compatibility of journeys and cargo windowsUsed only after receipt; the received time is part of the record
Booking lead time01Whether advance positioning is possible before pickupDerived from received time and requested pickup; never inferred from later information
Free-time interval02Whether an activity and trip fitUsed only under a consent purpose that covers suggestions
Optional preferences02, 03, 04Which offers are relevant; willingness to shift or shareOptional; absence or opt-out does not degrade the booking itself (SVC-004)

In data terms, a received plan enters through C01 as a PlanReference and is linked to a consent record carrying consentId, purpose and expiresAt together with the sourceEventId of the source (D02.1, P10 3.1). C02 holds the booking signals by planRefId. A calendar change produces a proposed intent, never a booking (BKG-063), and a calendar resync or deletion does not erase bookings (BKG-064).

Withdrawal or expiry stops further use of the signal for new positioning and offer decisions. The document does not state how withdrawal acts on a booking the user has already accepted; the intended separation is that accepted terms remain governed by the booking state model of P04 (cancellation is a user action, not a side effect of withdrawal), which keeps consent to information distinct from acceptance of terms. This is confirmed when consent ownership is agreed at G2 (TBD-050).

1.D.5 Use cases

One use case is defined per value mechanism. All share the preconditions that the requester is authenticated and admitted by C01, that the relevant consent is current, and that the service operates inside the selected geography and ODD agreed at MVP entry (SVC-026). Each use case ends in exactly one final disposition for every request (SVC-028).

UC1.1 Advance positioning. Goal: reduce wait and empty travel by moving reachable supply toward a pickup that is already known. Trigger: C02 receives a booking with sufficient lead time.

  1. C02 records the booking signal with its received time and consent scope (SVC-002).
  2. C03 evaluates reachable supply using only information received at decision time (SVC-003), within the energy capability supplied by C05.
  3. C04 positions the vehicle under a current D1 dispatch permit; the movement is recorded as part of the mission trace.
  4. The pickup is observed; pickup wait is computed from the C02 request and the C04 arrival (SVC-054), and empty travel from the mission trace.

Extensions: (a) the booking is cancelled after positioning — positioning, ETA and the recovery owner are updated (BKG-031), and the positioning travel is still counted as empty travel; (b) energy is insufficient — no positioning occurs and the booking proceeds without it; (c) the forecast is wrong — the positioning travel is counted as empty travel and the miss is retained for measurement; (d) execution becomes unknown — the affected capacity is not reused until reconciled (BKG-049).

UC1.2 Additional demand. Goal: offer an activity and a trip that fit a user's free time without displacing committed service. Trigger: a free-time interval is received under a consent purpose that covers suggestions.

  1. C02 requests activity slots from providers and transport feasibility from C03 for the interval.
  2. C03 returns a feasible bundle or a binding reason; providers return slot, price and capacity.
  3. C02 offers the combination with total price and expiry, only if all holds are valid (SVC-007, BKG-055).
  4. The user accepts; C02 commits the intent and the bundle (BKG-056); the provider confirms; observed use is reconciled by C07.

Extensions: (a) no feasible combination — no offer is made; (b) the user ignores or refuses the offer — the refusal or expiry is retained for measurement (SVC-055); (c) one hold is invalid or unknown — an owned exception releases the known holds (BKG-055); (d) the activity substitutes for a visit that would have happened anyway — this is not an error path but must be identified in measurement (SVC-049).

UC1.3 Demand smoothing. Goal: move an accepted trip within the user's flexible window to reduce peak load. Trigger: C03 identifies that a flexible accepted trip could move to a less loaded interval.

  1. C02 composes a revised offer within the flexible window, with the alternative total price (SVC-008).
  2. The original plan remains visible and valid while the offer is open (SVC-035).
  3. On acceptance, new capacity is held before the old allocation is retired, and the request keeps its identity (D02.2).
  4. Obsolete holds are released only after reconciliation (BKG-030).

Extensions: (a) the user declines or the offer expires — the original booking stands unchanged; (b) the new capacity cannot be held — the offer is withdrawn with a reason; (c) a revision conflict — terms are refreshed before any further acceptance (SVC-040).

UC1.4 Shared rides. Goal: carry compatible passenger journeys on one mission within each party's limits. Trigger: a request whose route overlaps an existing or candidate mission, from a user whose preferences permit sharing.

  1. C03 tests compatibility within seat, access and detour limits (SVC-009) and checks capacity on every route segment (BKG-004).
  2. C03 recomputes the limits of every passenger already on the route (BKG-005).
  3. C02 offers the sharing price and allowed detour explicitly (CAP-072); on acceptance each intent is linked to the route revision (BKG-032).
  4. C04 records one mission carrying several intents (SVC-012); each passenger's boarding and alighting is observed separately.

Extensions: (a) insertion would break any accepted limit — the match is not made; (b) a no-show or cancellation — the shared route is reconciled (CAP-074) and C06 owns passenger recovery (SVC-013). Detailed conditions: P29.

UC1.5 Passenger–freight sharing. Goal: use spare payload and space on passenger missions for eligible cargo. Trigger: an eligible shipment whose route and time window overlap a passenger mission.

  1. C03 checks payload, space, handling and time limits (SVC-010) and declines any cargo that would break a passenger commitment (CAP-084).
  2. Loading, custody and exception owners are assigned for the shipment (CAP-086).
  3. The shipment is linked to the route revision and its handovers are recorded (CAP-087).
  4. Delivery or failed-attempt proof is retained; C07 adds freight revenue and deducts added dwell and handling once.

Extensions: (a) the recipient is absent or the handover fails — C06 owns the cargo exception and return; failed handover is counted as consumed capacity (CAP-083); (b) cargo displaces a passenger trip — the displaced trip is reported, not hidden. Detailed conditions: P30.

1.D.6 Behaviour of the end-to-end service loop

All five mechanisms run on the same loop. The loop is specified once so that each mechanism is a variation of its inputs, not a separate product.

Main flow.

  1. Intent. The user shares a plan with consent through C01. C01 checks identity, object and tenant access, consent, schema and source cursor (PLT-001) and passes an authenticated command to C02. C02 records the intent and its consent scope. The request is idempotent (SVC-023).
  2. Feasible offer. C02 asks C03 to quote and hold. C03 combines the decision inputs — intent, reachable supply, provider slots, hub and energy limits — and returns either a feasible bundle with an expiry or a binding reason (SVC-024). C02 presents the offer with timing, total price and cancellation terms (SVC-036).
  3. Confirmed plan. The user accepts a specific terms revision. C02 commits all required holds before confirmation (BKG-029) and links each intent to its route revision.
  4. Trip and support. C04 obtains the current D1 permit before releasing a mission. The user sees state, ETA, data age and the help owner. Any exception is assigned an owner and a deadline (SVC-020).
  5. Verified outcome. C07 reconciles mission evidence, service actual and user outcome. Only a reconciled journey counts toward the north star (SVC-046).

Alternative flows. (1) No feasible capacity: stage 2 returns a binding reason and no promise is made (SVC-042). (2) User declines a revised offer: the original plan stands. (3) User cancels: the cancellation is recorded against the intent and follows P11 4.1; after permit issuance it becomes cancel or replan of an in-flight mission.

Exception flows. (1) A timeout or lost acknowledgement at any stage leaves the outcome unknown; the booking is queried and reconciled and no side effect is duplicated (SVC-039). (2) Stale evidence blocks the offer or action and returns the reason (SVC-041). (3) Capacity loss during the trip updates positioning, ETA and the recovery owner (BKG-031), and C06 owns passenger recovery.

The stage-by-stage interface calls are drawn in D01.1 and D02.1; the user-visible states are in D04.2.

1.D.7 Rules and invariants

The following rules bind all five mechanisms. They are the product-level invariants that the test cases in P24 and the gates in P07 check.

  1. R1.1 Purpose-bound signals. A signal is used only for the purpose recorded with its consent and only until its expiry or withdrawal (SVC-001).
  2. R1.2 No future information. Every positioning and offer decision uses only information received before the decision (SVC-003).
  3. R1.3 Acceptance before effect. A suggestion changes nothing until the user explicitly accepts it; no schedule changes automatically (SVC-005).
  4. R1.4 Accepted limits are binding. Seat, access, detour, payload, space, handling and time limits accepted by any party remain binding after any insertion (BKG-005, SVC-010).
  5. R1.5 Distinct identities. Each passenger and shipment intent remains a distinct identity through shared routes, revisions and outcomes (SVC-011).
  6. R1.6 One mission, many intents. A shared route is one vehicle mission; its distance and common costs are counted once (SVC-012, SVC-014).
  7. R1.7 Energy constrains supply. No supply is offered that the C05 energy capability does not support (SVC-015).
  8. R1.8 Owned exceptions. Every exception has an owner and a deadline; C06 owns passenger recovery and cargo exceptions (SVC-013, SVC-020).
  9. R1.9 Feasibility over contribution. Service feasibility and customer choice remain binding even when aggregate contribution would improve (SVC-075).
  10. R1.10 Separate attribution. Additional demand, shifted demand and shared-route efficiency are reported separately (SVC-049).

1.D.8 Measures

Each mechanism names a test measure and a limit. The measure states what would show the mechanism works; the limit states what would make an apparent gain misleading. Exact definitions are in P05 (D05.2); here they are stated in words to show how each mechanism is judged.

MechanismWhat success meansWhat would invalidate itP05 measures
01 Advance positioningUsers wait less, vehicles travel less empty, fewer requests go unserved, compared with the same demand without positioningPositioning that is wasted by cancellation, wrong forecast or insufficient energy, counted as empty travelPickup wait, empty travel, dispatch success, unserved demand
02 Additional demandUsers accept activities that they would not otherwise have made, and the net contribution is positiveSubstitution of visits that would have happened anyway; congestion induced by the extra tripsOffer conversion, additional trips, activity use, incremental contribution
03 Demand smoothingPeak load falls and missed pickups fall when accepted trips moveRefusals that leave peaks unchanged; discount cost that exceeds the benefitShift acceptance, peak demand, promise kept
04 Shared ridesMore passenger journeys per vehicle-hour within each party's accepted limitsDetour or wait beyond accepted limits; discounts that erase contributionPassenger output, seat-km utilization, detour, net contribution
05 Passenger–freight sharingFreight revenue added without breaking passenger commitmentsAdded dwell, displaced passenger trips, failed deliveries and returnsFreight delivery and lateness, cargo dwell, displaced passenger trips

Every measure is reported as a paired difference against a matched baseline (SVC-053); targets are set only once baseline evidence exists (SVC-048, TBD-031).

1.D.9 Experiment design and decision process

The hypothesis is tested in the sequence fixed by P05–P07. Before evaluation, each mechanism is completed with its outcome and failure condition in addition to the input, action, test and limit shown above (SVC-006); this belongs to G2 (DEFINE), whose check covers failure criteria (P07). Effects 01–03 are compared with matched inputs; 04 and 05 are compared in four conditions before interactions are tested (SVC-050, D05.3). Simulation runs are paired on initial conditions and seeds (SVC-057), and the stress sweep in P06 deliberately includes the limits listed per mechanism.

A mechanism advances only when its gain survives service guardrails, realistic acceptance, full costs and supply stress (SVC-030). The decision on each mechanism is recorded as continue, revise or stop in a decision packet (SVC-062); a mechanism whose effect is unsupported stays unvalidated rather than being reported as a partial gain.

1.D.10 Security, privacy and audit

  • Consent is checked at the boundary on every request (PLT-001) and again by independent guards before any automated proposal can act (OPS-090).
  • Source and receipt time, consent and custody evidence are preserved for each intent (SVC-019), so an auditor can reconstruct what the product knew, under which consent, at each decision.
  • All keys include tenant scope and references are validated within that scope (ASM-009), so records of one city partner or provider tenant are not joined to another's.
  • Optional preferences are minimised by design: the core booking works without them (SVC-004).
  • Retention periods and the legal basis for each purpose are reviewed before MVP entry as part of the legal and privacy review (SVC-026, TBD-048); this section sets no retention value.

1.D.11 Design rationale and alternatives considered

Five separable mechanisms rather than one optimisation objective. A single combined objective would make it impossible to tell which information or sharing effect produced a gain, and would allow a strong mechanism to hide a harmful one. Separate mechanisms with independent controls make each effect testable and stoppable on its own (SVC-030).

Consent per signal rather than blanket consent. Blanket consent would be simpler to implement but would make withdrawal all-or-nothing and would blur which purpose justified which decision. Per-signal purpose and expiry allow a user to share an intended arrival without sharing free time, and allow evidence to show that each decision used permitted information.

Suggestion with acceptance rather than automatic re-planning. Automatic re-planning could extract more shared capacity but would remove the user's control of timing and price, which is a stated property of the resident / visitor role. The design accepts lower acceptance as the cost of keeping choice binding (SVC-075).

Energy as a constraint rather than a stage. Placing C05 in the chain would imply that every booking waits for an energy decision. Treating energy capability as a versioned input to C03 feasibility keeps the booking path short and lets energy limit supply without owning bookings (BKG-008).

1.D.12 Open points

  • Outcome and failure condition for each mechanism — defined at G2 (SVC-006, P07 G2).
  • Consent, capacity and custody ownership — agreed at G2 (TBD-050).
  • ODD and access conditions set by the city partner — recorded in the G2 constraint register (TBD-011).
  • Shared-ride thresholds and cargo eligibility — TBD-029, TBD-047.
  • KPI targets — require baseline evidence (TBD-031).
  • Provider integration per provider — commercial API or owned manual workflow (TBD-039).

Passenger bookings, activity reservations and shipments retain distinct identities through shared routes, revised offers and verified outcomes.

2.DDetailed specification

This section specifies the service blueprint as an executable contract: for each of the five stages it defines who acts in each lane, the entry and exit conditions, the stage evidence that must exist before the next stage starts, and the alternative and exception paths. It then specifies the traceability key chain that keeps passenger bookings, activity reservations and shipments distinct through shared routes and revisions, and the acceptance invariants that every journey trace must satisfy.

2.D.1 Purpose and scope

The blueprint connects three lanes — what the user does, what the operator or provider does, and what the product platform records — across the stages Plan, Request, Confirm, Travel and Complete. Its purpose is to make the journey auditable end to end: at any point it must be possible to say what the user agreed to, what capacity was committed, what was observed and how the outcome was reconciled.

The section covers a single journey and its revisions, including journeys that share a vehicle mission with other passengers or with cargo. It does not specify the internal booking saga, reservation transactions or mission execution; those are in P09, P10, P11 and P13. The activity-provider side of a combined journey follows P23 16.1.

2.D.2 Users and scenarios

The blueprint is written for three journey shapes that share one record model:

Single-party trip
One passenger booking, one route revision, one mission. The key chain is one-to-one throughout.
Trip with activity
A passenger booking combined with an activity reservation from a provider. The provider and transport reservations are not one distributed transaction (ASM-008); the blueprint keeps them as separate holds under one accepted terms revision.
Shared mission
Several passenger bookings, and possibly shipments, on one vehicle mission. Each keeps its own intent and outcome while the route and its costs are shared.

In each shape the same failures recur: the user changes the plan, the user cancels, capacity is lost, or an acknowledgement does not arrive. The blueprint treats these as defined paths with their own evidence, not as exceptions to be cleaned up later.

2.D.3 Actors and responsibilities per stage

Each cell names the lane's responsibility at that stage and the component that carries it on the platform side. The user lane is served through C01 and the user app (P04); the operator / provider lane through the consoles behind I02 and I06 (I02, I06).

StageUserOperator / providerProduct / platformPlatform owner
1 PlanShares plan, time and preferences under consentReads received booking signals; validates that only known information is usedRecords consent and signal receiptC01 (PlanReference), C02
2 RequestCompares activity, travel and priceChecks seats, cargo and time limits; feasibility against supply, ODD, slots and energyChecks capacity on each route segmentC03, with C05 capability
3 ConfirmAccepts timing and total termsCommits route, slots and handoff; revision check on resource holdsLinks each intent to the route revisionC02 (D1), C03 (D2)
4 TravelTracks status; requests helpMonitors the trip and owns exceptions; recovers from a missing acknowledgement by query or re-planPublishes current state and caseC04 (D3), C06
5 CompleteConfirms trip and activity useVerifies passenger and cargo outcomes; reconciles intent outcome, usage and costReconciles fares, freight and costsC07 (D6)

2.D.4 Preconditions and inputs

  • The requester is admitted by C01: identity, object and tenant access, consent, schema and source cursor are checked (PLT-001).
  • The journey lies within the geography, ODD, channel and segment selected at MVP entry (SVC-026).
  • Provider, fleet and site capacity for the slice has been confirmed, and service and incident owners are named (SVC-026).
  • Inputs to feasibility are those listed in P09 2.1: passenger and cargo time windows; party, access, mass and volume; detour, handling and consent; and the policy version and snapshot time (BKG-001).

2.D.5 Behaviour

Stage contract. Each stage has an entry condition and produces stage evidence; the next stage may begin only when that evidence exists. This turns the blueprint into a checkable sequence rather than a picture.

StageEntry conditionStage evidence (exit)If evidence is missing
1 PlanAuthenticated request with consentConsent + receipt time recorded (SVC-002)Signal is not used for any decision
2 RequestPlan evidence exists; inputs known at decision timeEligible offer + capacity: a feasible bundle with expiry, or a binding reason (SVC-024)No offer; reason returned (SVC-041)
3 ConfirmOffer not expired; terms revision currentAccepted terms + committed holds (BKG-029)Booking is not confirmed; terms are refreshed on revision conflict (SVC-040)
4 TravelBooking confirmed; current D1 permitObserved pickup + owned exception, if any (SVC-020)Mission is not released; unknown execution blocks reuse (BKG-049)
5 CompleteMission ended or exception closedTrip / activity actuals + cost (SVC-018)Journey stays unreconciled and does not count (SVC-046)

Main flow — confirmed journey.

  1. The user shares a plan, time window and preferences. C01 stores a PlanReference with its source and consent; C02 receives the booking signals by planRefId.
  2. The operator lane validates the signals: only information already received is used, and nothing that arrives later is back-filled into this decision (SVC-003).
  3. C02 requests a quote and hold from C03 over I03 (I03). C03 checks seats, accessible space, payload and cargo volume on every segment (BKG-004) and returns a held bundle with holdId and expiresAt, or a binding reason.
  4. C02 presents the offer: activity and trip, total price and expiry.
  5. The user accepts a specific termsRev. C02 persists the intent with COMMIT_PENDING and its outbox in D1, then commits the bundle; on a durable outcome C02 sets CONFIRMED by compare-and-set and links the intent to the route revision (BKG-032).
  6. C04 obtains the current D1 permit, releases the mission over I04 (I04) and publishes MissionObserved. The user sees ETA and data age, and the name of the help owner.
  7. Boarding, alighting or delivery is observed per passenger and per shipment. C07 receives units and quality over I08 (I08), reconciles fares, freight and costs and publishes UsageVerified.
  8. The user receives the outcome: trip or activity, and any refund status.

The same flow as interface calls is drawn in D02.1.

Alternative flow — revised plan or time shift.

  1. The user accepts revised terms through I02 amend. The request keeps its identity: a time shift is a revision of the same intent, not a new request.
  2. C02 persists the amended intent and outbox in D1.
  3. C03 holds the new capacity first, referencing the bundle it replaces, and rechecks every route segment.
  4. C03 swaps the allocation only where the old allocation has not started; a started or unknown mission retains its occupancy until physical clearance (BKG-038).
  5. Obsolete holds are released only after reconciliation (BKG-030).

If the user declines the revision, nothing changes: the original plan remains visible and valid (SVC-035).

Exception flows.

  1. Cancellation. The user cancels against the intent and current revision. C02 records the cancellation, C03 reconciles or cancels the allocation, and positioning, ETA and the recovery owner are updated (BKG-031). After permit issuance, cancellation becomes cancel or replan of an in-flight mission (P11 4.1).
  2. Capacity loss. A vehicle, hub or energy limit removes committed capacity. C04 reports the ETA change; C03 reconciles; C06 assigns a recovery owner with a deadline; the affected user receives a customer outcome.
  3. Missing acknowledgement. A commit, mission or energy response does not return. The effect is treated as unknown, never as rejected (PLT-044); the platform queries the original intent and reconciles before any retry with a different payload (SVC-039, BKG-026).
  4. Failed cargo handover or no-show. The shared route is reconciled (CAP-074); C06 owns passenger recovery and the cargo exception (SVC-013).

These paths are drawn in D02.2.

2.D.6 Use cases

UC2.1 Complete a planned journey. Goal: the user travels as accepted and the outcome is reconciled. Trigger: the user shares a plan. Main success scenario: the main flow above. Postcondition: one final disposition for the request, linked to observed evidence and one cost record (SVC-028). Extensions: the offer expires before acceptance (the hold is released and the request ends without a booking); no feasible option exists (a binding reason is shown).

UC2.2 Accept a revised plan. Goal: the user moves to a better plan without losing the original until the new one is secure. Trigger: a revised offer from mechanism 02, 03 or 04. Main success scenario: the alternative flow above. Extensions: the new hold fails (the original stays); a revision conflict occurs (terms are refreshed before acceptance is possible).

UC2.3 Recover from cancellation or capacity loss. Goal: every affected party has an owner, a deadline and a communicated outcome. Trigger: a cancellation, no-show or capacity loss. Main success scenario: exception flows 1, 2 and 4. Extension: recovery itself fails — the case remains owned and the failure is recorded separately (SVC-045).

UC2.4 Resolve an unknown effect. Goal: an unknown outcome is resolved without duplicating any side effect. Trigger: a timeout or lost acknowledgement. Main success scenario: exception flow 3. Extension: the outcome stays unknown until its deadline — it is retained as an owned exception with a backup owner and fallback (OPS-097).

2.D.7 Data and state

Traceability key chain. The chain intentId + passenger / shipmentId + bookingRev + routeRev + missionId is carried on every journey record (SVC-016). Its parts have different owners and different cardinalities, which is what allows sharing without merging identities (D02.3).

KeyOwnerFirst required atChanges whenCardinality
intentIdC022 RequestNever; preserved across time shifts and revisionsOne per request
passenger / shipmentIdC022 RequestNeverOne per party or cargo item within an intent
bookingRevC02 / D13 ConfirmEvery accepted amendment or cancellation; updated by compare-and-set against expectedBookingRevAdvances with each accepted change of the booking
routeRevC03 / D23 Confirm (intent linked to route revision)Every insertion, removal or reordering of stopsShared by all intents on the route
missionIdC04 / D34 TravelNever for a given missionOne per vehicle mission; several intents may reference it

Records kept. Offers, accepted terms, original and revised times, route stops and segment occupancy are recorded (SVC-017). Every passenger and shipment is linked to observed boarding, alighting or delivery (SVC-018). Source and receipt time, consent and custody evidence are preserved per intent (SVC-019). Shared mission costs remain unique: a cost is attached to the mission once and allocated to intents, never duplicated per intent (SVC-014).

State. The user-visible booking states are defined in P04 (D04.2); reservation states in D2 in P09 2.3; booking saga states in D1 in P11 4.1. The blueprint does not introduce further states. Stage evidence is not a state: it is the set of records whose presence allows the next stage to begin.

Writers. Each entity has one writing component (PLT-009); other components consume its events through an idempotent inbox (PLT-015). The blueprint's cross-lane hand-offs therefore never write another component's record directly.

2.D.8 Rules and invariants

The acceptance invariants are restated as numbered rules with the requirement each corresponds to. A journey trace that violates any of them fails acceptance.

  1. R2.1 Positioning uses information already received (SVC-003).
  2. R2.2 All required holds are committed before confirmation (BKG-029).
  3. R2.3 Seats, accessible space, payload and cargo volume are checked on every segment (BKG-004).
  4. R2.4 Existing passenger limits are recomputed after any insertion and remain binding (BKG-005).
  5. R2.5 A time shift preserves request identity (SVC-011).
  6. R2.6 A suggestion needs acceptance before it takes effect (SVC-005).
  7. R2.7 An unknown effect requires reconciliation and never produces a duplicate side effect (SVC-039).
  8. R2.8 Completion uses passenger and cargo evidence separately (SVC-018).
  9. R2.9 Each exception retains an owner and a deadline (SVC-020).
  10. R2.10 A revised plan releases obsolete holds only after reconciliation (BKG-030).
  11. R2.11 Cancellation or capacity loss updates positioning, ETA and the recovery owner (BKG-031).

2.D.9 Interfaces used

StageInterfaceUse in the blueprint
1 PlanI01Resident and partner channel for plans, preferences and consent
2–3I02, I03Commit, amend and cancel of bookings; quote, hold and atomic replacement of capacity
2–3I06Provider console for activity slots and confirmations
4 TravelI04, I07Mission, receipt and execution; case actions by type
5 CompleteI08Units, quality and correction links for settlement
AllC09BookingChanged, AllocationCommitted, MissionObserved, UsageVerified and CaseChanged between lanes

Payload examples are conceptual, not complete schemas (ASM-005, TBD-040); protocols beyond those stated are open (TBD-003).

2.D.10 Failure handling and recovery

The blueprint relies on three recovery principles that are specified elsewhere and applied here at journey level.

  • Unknown is not failure. A missing acknowledgement leaves the effect unknown; the dispatch permit stays blocked (DSP-004), and the reservation moves to RECONCILING and queries the original intent (BKG-026). Retrying with the same idempotency key is safe; the same key with a different payload is rejected (PLT-042).
  • Hold new before releasing old. A revision never leaves the user without capacity: old capacity is released only after the new is committed and reconciled (BKG-030), and physical capacity only after clearance (BKG-038).
  • Owned exceptions. Every failure becomes a case with an owner and deadline; if the deadline passes with the outcome still unknown, the case is retained with a backup owner and fallback rather than closed (OPS-097).

After a platform restore, journeys pass through RESTORE → RECONCILE → ENABLE DISPATCH before any mission is released (P08 1.2); replay uses separate projections so that no user-visible side effect is repeated (PLT-017).

2.D.11 Security, privacy and audit

  • The consent record is part of stage 1 evidence; a later stage that uses a signal can cite the consent that permitted it.
  • Custody evidence is kept per shipment so that a failed handover can be attributed to a stage and an owner.
  • All keys include tenant scope and references are validated within that scope (ASM-009); intents on a shared mission are joined through routeRev and missionId, not by merging their records.
  • Raw observation events and validation results are kept append-only (OPS-086); together with the stage evidence they form the audit trail, and no stage overwrites the evidence of an earlier stage.

2.D.12 Verification approach

The blueprint is verified by journey traces rather than by component tests alone. Each trace is a complete key chain with its stage evidence, checked against R2.1–R2.11.

TraceWhat it showsGate / fault case
Normal journey, single partyEvery stage evidence present; one disposition; one cost recordG3
Revised planIdentity preserved; new hold before old release; obsolete holds released after reconciliationG3
Shared mission with cargoPer-segment limits; separate passenger and cargo evidence; costs counted onceG3 (SVC-068)
Cancellation and capacity lossPositioning, ETA and recovery owner updated; customer outcome sentG3 (SVC-027)
Lost acknowledgementUnknown reconciled; no duplicate effectT-R04

The fault-injection cases that exercise these traces are planned in P24; they are planned tests, not passed results (ASM-030).

2.D.13 Design rationale and alternatives considered

A composite key chain rather than one journey identifier. A single journey identifier would be simpler but would force either a new identifier on every revision (losing request identity) or one identifier across shared passengers (merging identities). Separating request identity, booking revision, route revision and mission lets each change at its own rate while remaining joinable.

Stage evidence as the gate between stages. Allowing stages to proceed on optimistic assumptions would shorten the path but would produce journeys whose outcome cannot be reconstructed. Requiring evidence before the next stage costs latency in the exception paths only; the normal path already produces the evidence.

Saga with reconciliation rather than one transaction. Provider, transport and energy reservations live in different systems. A distributed atomic commit is not assumed (ASM-007); instead each external effect is reconciled, and unknown effects keep capacity blocked. This is slower to resolve in rare cases but does not depend on every partner supporting a common transaction protocol.

2.D.14 Open points

  • Complete schemas for the records and interfaces used here (TBD-040).
  • Per-provider support for hold, commit and cancel, or an owned manual workflow (TBD-039).
  • Freshness budgets for status shown in stage 4 (TBD-006, decided at G2).
  • Query budget for unresolved commands (TBD-027).
  • Custody ownership for cargo — agreed at G2 (TBD-050).

Mobility service planning / Product management supplementP03 / 30

MVP boundary and product prioritization

A complete service slice provides the baseline. Five controlled mechanisms test information value and shared-capacity economics.

03MVP & prioritization

Priority rule

Rank by measured service benefit, net contribution, feasibility and learning value.

Common fleet / hubs / demand conditions support comparison. Capacity and service guardrails remain binding.

Dependency orderReliable request / outcome records precede effect measurement. Finite capacity and recovery precede offer expansion.

Pilot MVP

One selected service slice

  1. 01Capture intent, needs, consent and idempotent request
  2. 02Return feasible options, binding reasons and expiry
  3. 03Commit booking + resource bundle with revision checks
  4. 04Track state, freshness, support case and recovery owner
  5. 05Reconcile actual trip, service use and passenger outcome

Exit only when normal + recovery paths pass acceptance; operator can resolve exceptions; event and cost records reconcile.
Required evidence: valid, rejected, cancelled and recovered journeys. Reconcile every request to one final disposition and every cost to one owner.

Iterate

Five controlled mechanisms

  1. 01Use received plans for feasible advance positioning
  2. 02Offer activities within spare time and capacity
  3. 03Shift accepted trips with clear timing and price
  4. 04Pool compatible riders within each detour limit
  5. 05Insert eligible cargo within payload and time limits

Advance when gains survive service guardrails, realistic acceptance, full costs and supply stress.
Retain independent controls for all five effects. Test late signals, substitution, peak overload, no-shows, cargo dwell and failed handovers.

Extend platform

Repeatable operating model

  1. 01Versioned adapters and purpose-limited consent
  2. 02Energy, hub throughput and staffing in feasibility
  3. 03Guarded support and owned passenger recovery
  4. 04Calibrate by zone, time and user segment
  5. 05Reusable configuration, evidence and rollback

Expand after second-site tests preserve service quality and net contribution with local demand, capacity and operating costs. Replication tests: different OD pattern, provider capacity, support load and energy limits. Retain tenant isolation and configuration / policy versions.

MVP control

MVP entry criteria: selected geography / ODD / channel / segment; named service and incident owners; provider, fleet and site capacity confirmed; legal, privacy, accessibility and partner constraints reviewed; C01–C07 data and authority boundaries agreed. Pilot exit: normal + cancellation + disruption / recovery traces pass; queue and support coverage are staffed; KPI baseline, missing-data behavior and cost ledger reconcile; rollback and customer communication are rehearsed. Optional C05 optimization, remote assistance and I09 roadside sensing stay out until separately gated.

G2 constraint register: ODD = approved operating conditions (road, speed, weather, time, etc.). DDT = real-time operational / tactical functions needed to operate in traffic (including OEDR); record which actor performs them. Define DDT fallback separately by actor, trigger, response and intervention boundary. Also record operating limits (hours / staffing / recovery), infrastructure (node power / energy / footprint) and business limits (fare / demand / transit overlap). For each, record variable, unit / value or TBD, source URL, owner, affected KPI and PL line. Set thresholds only after evidence and ownership are confirmed. Source: SAE J3016_202609, doi:10.4271/J3016_202609.

3.DDetailed specification

This section specifies how product work is scoped, ordered and admitted. It defines the priority rule and the dependency order as decision procedures, the pilot MVP as a complete service slice with acceptance evidence per step, the entry and exit criteria that bound the pilot, the iterate and extend stages as evidence-gated progressions, and the G2 constraint register as the record that holds every operating, infrastructure and business limit until evidence and ownership allow a value to be set.

3.D.1 Purpose and scope

The chapter answers two questions that determine everything that follows: what is the smallest service that can be operated and measured end to end, and in what order may capability be added to it. The answer is a staged progression — pilot MVP, iterate, extend platform — in which each stage has a defined content and an exit condition, and in which the five value mechanisms of P01 are introduced only after the baseline service is reliable.

In scope are the priority rule, the dependency order, the content of the three stages, MVP entry and pilot exit, the scope excluded from the MVP and the G2 constraint register. The gate definitions themselves (G1–G5, GO / HOLD / REVISE) are specified in P07; this section uses them and states how the three stages align with them (D03.1).

3.D.2 Users and scenarios

The users of this chapter are the people who decide scope, not the passengers. Three decision scenarios recur:

Choosing the next item of work
Several candidate improvements compete for the same engineering and operations capacity. The priority rule ranks them; the dependency order removes those whose prerequisites are not yet in place.
Deciding whether the pilot can start
Partners, fleet and site are being prepared. MVP entry criteria determine whether the slice is defined well enough to operate and measure.
Deciding whether a mechanism or a site can be added
A mechanism shows a gain in simulation, or a second site is proposed. The iterate and extend exit conditions decide whether the evidence is sufficient.

3.D.3 Actors and responsibilities

Decision ownership follows P07 Product decision ownership (SVC-073). For the work in this chapter, it resolves as follows.

RoleDecides or verifies in this chapter
PMRanking of product work; selection of geography, ODD, channel and segment; KPI decisions at pilot exit
DesignComprehension and accessibility of the MVP flows; accessibility review at entry
EngineeringC01–C07 data and authority boundaries; trace quality; normal and fault-path acceptance; rollback
Operations / partnersProvider, fleet and site capacity; queue and support staffing; recovery
FinanceCost ledger reconciliation; revenue scope and cost allocation used in net contribution
Named service and incident ownersAccountable for the operating pilot; required at entry

Every HOLD raised against a stage has a named closure owner (SVC-074); an entry or exit criterion without an owner is itself a reason to hold.

3.D.4 Priority rule

Product work is ranked by four criteria: measured service benefit, net contribution, feasibility and learning value (SVC-021). The rule is applied as a two-step procedure.

  1. Filter. Remove any candidate that would weaken a capacity or service guardrail. Guardrails are binding constraints, not criteria to be traded: a candidate that improves contribution by relaxing an accepted service limit is not ranked at all (SVC-075).
  2. Rank. Compare the remaining candidates on the four criteria, using estimates obtained under common fleet, hub and demand conditions so that the comparison is not distorted by different assumptions.

Learning value is a criterion in its own right because, early in the programme, a small item that resolves an uncertain assumption can be worth more than a larger item whose benefit is already understood. Measured benefit means benefit observed or simulated under the matched comparison of P06, not an expected value asserted without evidence. The relative weighting of the four criteria is not fixed in the document; it is a PM decision recorded with the evidence used.

3.D.5 Dependency order

Two dependencies constrain the order regardless of rank (SVC-022):

  1. Records before measurement. Reliable request and outcome records must exist before any effect is measured. An effect estimated on incomplete or unreconciled records cannot be distinguished from a recording artefact.
  2. Capacity and recovery before expansion. Finite capacity checks and recovery must exist before offers are expanded. Expanding offers without them would create promises the service cannot keep and failures nobody owns.

A highly ranked item whose dependency is not satisfied waits; the dependency itself becomes the item of work.

3.D.6 Pilot MVP: one selected service slice

The pilot MVP is a complete slice: every stage of the service loop exists for one selected geography, ODD, channel and user segment. None of the five value mechanisms is required in it. Its role is to provide the baseline against which mechanisms are later compared.

StepCapabilityComponentsAcceptance evidenceRequirement
01Capture intent, needs and consent through an idempotent requestC01, C02Repeated submission yields one intent; consent scope and receipt time recordedSVC-023
02Return feasible options, binding reasons and expiryC02, C03Every quote has an expiry; every infeasible request has a binding reasonSVC-024
03Commit booking and resource bundle with revision checksC02, C03No confirmation without all holds committed; stale revisions rejectedBKG-029; PLT-041
04Track state, freshness, support case and recovery ownerC02, C04, C06Each journey shows state, evidence age, case and ownerSVC-025
05Reconcile actual trip, service use and passenger outcomeC04, C07Each request has one final disposition; each cost one ownerSVC-028

The pilot slice uses the booking, reservation and dispatch contracts of P09–P11 without the optional extensions excluded below. The mapping of steps to traces is in D03.2.

3.D.7 Behaviour: MVP entry, operation and pilot exit

Main flow.

  1. Prepare. PM selects geography, ODD, channel and segment; the service and incident owners are named; Operations confirms provider, fleet and site capacity.
  2. Review constraints. Legal, privacy, accessibility and partner constraints are reviewed; each limit that affects the slice is entered in the G2 constraint register (3.D.10).
  3. Agree boundaries. Engineering records the C01–C07 data and authority boundaries for the slice: which component writes which record, and which actor may trigger which action.
  4. Enter. When all entry criteria hold (SVC-026), the pilot starts within the selected slice only.
  5. Operate. The slice runs steps 01–05. Normal, cancellation and disruption / recovery journeys are recorded as traces.
  6. Exit. The pilot exits when the normal, cancellation and disruption / recovery traces pass; queue and support coverage are staffed; the KPI baseline, missing-data behaviour and cost ledger reconcile; and rollback and customer communication have been rehearsed (SVC-027). Required evidence includes valid, rejected, cancelled and recovered journeys (SVC-028).

Alternative flows. (1) An entry criterion is not met: the pilot does not start; the missing item is assigned an owner and a deadline as a REVISE outcome (SVC-065). (2) Capacity confirmed at entry is later withdrawn by a partner: new offers in the slice are restricted while accepted journeys are protected, consistent with constrained operation in P27.

Exception flows. (1) A trace reveals duplicated intents, unreconciled costs or an unowned exception: pilot exit is held and the scope stays restricted until the named owner closes the gap (SVC-066). (2) A safety, privacy or legal risk is found during operation: the gate holds (SVC-064) and the rehearsed rollback and customer communication are used.

Excluded scope. Optional C05 optimization, remote assistance and I09 roadside sensing stay outside the MVP until separately gated (SVC-029; TBD-022, TBD-023, TBD-021). Exclusion does not remove C05 as a constraint: energy capability still limits feasible supply (SVC-015); what is excluded is optimization beyond that constraint.

3.D.8 Iterate: five controlled mechanisms

Each mechanism is added to the baseline slice with its own control, so that it can be switched on and off independently. The table states, for each, what is introduced and which stress cases from the chapter it must survive.

MechanismIntroduced capabilityRequirementStress cases emphasised
01 PositioningUse received plans for feasible advance positioningSVC-003Late signals; cancellation after positioning
02 ActivitiesOffer activities within spare time and capacitySVC-007Substitution; peak overload
03 Time shiftShift accepted trips with clear timing and priceSVC-008Refusal; peak overload
04 PoolingPool compatible riders within each detour limitSVC-009No-shows; peak overload
05 CargoInsert eligible cargo within payload and time limitsSVC-010Cargo dwell; failed handovers

A mechanism advances when its gains survive service guardrails, realistic acceptance, full costs and supply stress (SVC-030); this aligns with G4. Independent controls are retained for all five effects even after a mechanism advances, because later interaction tests (SVC-050) need each effect to be switchable on the same baseline.

3.D.9 Extend platform: repeatable operating model

Extension turns the validated slice into something that can be repeated at another site. Its five items are prerequisites for replication rather than new user features:

  1. Versioned adapters and purpose-limited consent, so that a new site connects through the same contracts and consent purposes remain explicit.
  2. Energy, hub throughput and staffing included in feasibility, so that local limits enter C03 as constraints (P25–P26).
  3. Guarded support and owned passenger recovery (P21, P27).
  4. Calibration by zone, time and user segment, so that acceptance and demand assumptions are local.
  5. Reusable configuration, evidence and rollback.

Expansion follows only after second-site tests preserve service quality and net contribution with local demand, capacity and operating costs, with tenant isolation and configuration / policy versions retained (SVC-031); this aligns with G5 (SVC-069). The replication tests deliberately vary OD pattern, provider capacity, support load and energy limits so that a gain that depended on the first site's conditions is exposed.

3.D.10 Data and state: the G2 constraint register

The register is the single record of every limit under which the service may operate. It exists so that no limit is introduced implicitly in code or configuration without a source, an owner and a link to the measures it affects (D03.3).

Constraint classes
ODD; DDT and the actor that performs it; DDT fallback; operating limits (hours / staffing / recovery); infrastructure limits (node power / energy / footprint); business limits (fare / demand / transit overlap).
Fields per entry
Variable; unit / value or TBD; source URL; owner; affected KPI; PL line (SVC-032).
DDT entry
Records which actor performs the DDT, including OEDR. In this baseline the Level 4 ADS retains DDT and fallback authority (ASM-010).
DDT fallback entry
Defined separately by actor, trigger, response and intervention boundary (SVC-033, TBD-012).

Value lifecycle. An entry is created with its value marked TBD. The value is set only after evidence and ownership are confirmed (SVC-034); until then, any component that depends on it treats the limit as not yet established and the slice cannot rely on it. A value is never inferred from a default or from another site. Each entry's link to an affected KPI and PL line means that changing a limit is visible as a change in what is measured and in the financial model, not only in operation.

The entries that the document leaves open are tracked as TBD-011 (ODD), TBD-012 (DDT and fallback), TBD-013 (operating), TBD-014 (infrastructure) and TBD-015 (business). Terminology follows the baseline cited in the chapter (ASM-034).

3.D.11 Rules and invariants

  1. R3.1 Guardrails filter candidates before ranking; they are never weighed against contribution (SVC-021, SVC-075).
  2. R3.2 Candidates are compared under common fleet, hub and demand conditions (SVC-021).
  3. R3.3 No effect is measured before reliable request and outcome records exist; no offer is expanded before finite capacity and recovery exist (SVC-022).
  4. R3.4 The pilot starts only when every entry criterion holds (SVC-026).
  5. R3.5 Every request reconciles to one final disposition and every cost to one owner (SVC-028).
  6. R3.6 Optional C05 optimization, remote assistance and I09 roadside sensing stay out of the MVP until separately gated (SVC-029).
  7. R3.7 Each mechanism keeps an independent control through the iterate and extend stages (SVC-030).
  8. R3.8 A constraint value stays TBD until evidence and ownership are confirmed (SVC-034).
  9. R3.9 A failed condition returns the work to the earliest gate whose assumption is invalidated (SVC-066).

3.D.12 Decision process

The three stages are not calendar phases. Each exit is a gate decision taken on evidence (SVC-063):

DecisionAligned gateGO whenHOLD / REVISE when
Pilot exitG3 / Pilot readyNormal and recovery paths pass; operator can resolve exceptions; event and cost records reconcileAny trace fails; support unstaffed; costs unreconciled
Advance a mechanismG4 / LearnGain survives guardrails, realistic acceptance, full costs and supply stressGain disappears under stress or costs; a guardrail breaks
ExpandG5 / RepeatSecond-site tests preserve service quality and net contributionGains depend on first-site conditions; local limits break service

A REVISE outcome names an owner, the required evidence, a deadline and a temporary scope restriction, and records the rollback trigger and resume authority (SVC-065). The gate flow is drawn in D03.1; the GO / HOLD record fields are in P07 (SVC-070).

3.D.13 Verification approach

  • Entry: inspection of the entry checklist against named owners and the constraint register (D03.2).
  • Pilot steps 01–05: test of each step's acceptance evidence in 3.D.6, including duplicate submission, expired quotes, stale revisions and lost acknowledgements (T-R04).
  • Exit: demonstration of normal, cancellation and disruption / recovery traces with staffed support, and reconciliation of the cost ledger and KPI baseline; rollback and customer communication rehearsed (SVC-027).
  • Iterate: analysis by paired simulation and stress sweep (P06), then bounded field checks.
  • Extend: demonstration at a second site under the replication tests.

3.D.14 Design rationale and alternatives considered

Complete thin slice rather than feature-first MVP. An MVP built around one attractive mechanism (for example pooling) would show early gains but would have no reliable baseline against which to measure them and no recovery path when sharing fails. A complete slice delays the first mechanism but makes every later measurement interpretable.

Guardrails as filters rather than criteria. Treating service limits as weighted criteria would allow a large contribution gain to outweigh a broken commitment. Making them filters keeps the user-facing promise independent of the business case, as required by the decision basis in P07.

TBD as a recorded value rather than a provisional number. Entering a provisional threshold would let design proceed faster but would hide which limits are actually unsupported. Recording TBD with an owner and the affected KPI makes the gap visible in reviews and prevents an unvalidated value from being mistaken for an approved one.

Exclusion of optional capabilities. Energy optimization, remote assistance and roadside sensing each bring their own safety, partner and evidence requirements. Keeping them out of the MVP keeps the pilot's failure modes within the booking-to-settlement chain that the MVP is designed to measure.

3.D.15 Open points

  • MVP entry items: selected slice, owners, capacity and boundaries (TBD-048).
  • All G2 constraint register values (TBD-011–TBD-015).
  • Separate gating of optional C05 optimization, remote assistance and I09 roadside sensing (TBD-021–TBD-023).
  • Relative weighting of the four priority criteria — a PM decision; no value is set in the document.
  • KPI targets — require the baseline established at pilot exit (TBD-031).

4.DDetailed specification

This section specifies the interaction concept as behaviour: the content, validation and actions of each user-app screen, the choice rule that protects the user's original plan, the user-visible booking state model with its entry and exit conditions, the operator workspace as a set of permitted actions each bound to its context and guard, the handling of unknown, stale and conflicting states in both surfaces, and the usability test design that decides whether the concept is understood and safe to operate.

4.D.1 Purpose and scope

The interaction concept exposes the booking and capacity contracts of the platform to two audiences with different needs. The resident or visitor needs a short request–offer–service path in which every meaningful choice is visible and nothing changes without consent. The operator needs the context that explains each offer and a bounded set of actions that cannot break a commitment. Both surfaces are views of the same records; neither holds authoritative state.

In scope are the three app screens, the choice rule, the user-visible state model, the operator workspace, the usability tasks and the prototype evidence. Visual design, layout and platform-specific interaction are outside this specification and are left to Design, which owns comprehension and accessibility (SVC-073). The remote-operation HMI for vehicle incidents is a separate surface specified in P21.

4.D.2 Users and scenarios

Resident with an access need
Books a trip with a wheelchair space and luggage. Needs to see that the offered vehicle meets the access need on every segment and that a sharing option will not remove it.
Visitor comparing options
Receives an activity offer and a time-shift offer while already holding a booking. Needs to compare each against the original and decline without losing it.
Passenger during service
Sees that the vehicle is late. Needs current state, the age of the information and a way to reach help.
Operator at peak
Sees demand exceeding reachable supply in one zone. Needs to stop making new promises there while protecting accepted trips, and to explain each rejection.
Operator after a lost acknowledgement
A commit has not been confirmed. Needs to resolve it without creating a second booking or a second charge.

4.D.3 Actors and responsibilities

Actor / componentResponsibility in the interaction
User appCollects the request, presents offers and state, submits acceptances, declines, cancellations and help requests. Displays only what C02 and C04 have published; never infers a state.
Operator workspacePresents capacity, queue and offer context; issues permitted actions through C02, C03 and C06. Shows the reason for any blocked action.
C01Admits each request from both surfaces: identity, tenant access, consent, schema (PLT-001).
C02Owns the booking, its terms revision and its user-visible state; the single writer for booking records.
C03Evaluates feasibility, holds and commits capacity; returns binding reasons.
C04Publishes mission state, ETA and pickup / onboard / arrival evidence.
C06Owns help requests, recovery and cargo exceptions as cases with severity and dueAt.

4.D.4 User-app screens

Each screen corresponds to one stage of the request–offer–service flow and to a set of booking states. Detail is shown when the user compares or changes a plan, not by default.

ScreenContentValidation / guardUser actionsStates shown
01 Request — plan a journeyOrigin / destination and pickup point; time window and allowed detour; party, access and luggage needs; consent and sharing preferenceFields validated before submission; optional data stays optional (SVC-004); submission is idempotent (SVC-023)Validate → submit intentDRAFT
02 Offer — choose a feasible planActivity / trip and sharing option; pickup / arrival and detour limit; seat / access and cargo compatibility; total price and discount / refundTiming, total price and cancellation terms confirmed before acceptance (SVC-036); offer shown with its expiryAccept plan / keep originalQUOTED, PENDING
03 Service — track and get helpBooking / mission state and age; ETA and last update; pickup / onboard / arrival proofState and age come from published records onlyHelp, cancel or recovery path; confirm outcome / recoverCONFIRMED, IN_SERVICE, COMPLETED, CANCELLED

Request screen behaviour. The allowed detour and the sharing preference are captured at request time because they are the limits that later sharing offers must respect; they cannot be widened by an offer without a new acceptance. Access and luggage needs are captured per party so that seat and accessible-space checks can be applied per segment (BKG-004).

Offer screen behaviour. When no feasible option exists, the screen shows the binding reason and makes no promise (SVC-042). When the user already holds a booking, the offer is shown beside the original, never in place of it (SVC-035). Each option shows its total price, including discount or refund, so that the user compares totals rather than components.

Service screen behaviour. State is always shown with its age. An ETA without a last-update time is not shown as current. Help is reachable from every service state, and the screen names who owns the user's case once one exists.

4.D.5 Choice rule

  1. R4.1 Original stays visible. While a revised plan is offered, the original plan remains visible and accessible (SVC-035).
  2. R4.2 Decline keeps the original. Declining, ignoring or letting a revised offer expire leaves the original booking unchanged (SVC-035).
  3. R4.3 Terms before acceptance. Timing, total price and cancellation terms are confirmed before acceptance (SVC-036); acceptance refers to the terms revision that was shown.
  4. R4.4 No automatic change. No schedule changes automatically and consent is never forced (SVC-005, SVC-004; ASM-026).

4.D.6 Data and state: user-visible booking state model

The state model is what the user sees (SVC-037). It is a view of the booking held by C02; the reservation states of P09 2.3 and the D1 saga states of P11 4.1 remain internal. The diagram and transition table are in D04.2.

StateMeaning to the userEntered whenLeft whenUser may
DRAFTRequest being composedUser starts a requestIntent submitted and quotedEdit, submit
QUOTEDA feasible offer exists until expiresAtC03 returns a feasible bundleUser accepts, or the offer expires, or a revision conflict refreshes the termsCompare, accept, keep original
PENDINGAcceptance received; capacity heldUser accepts the shown termsCommit outcome is knownWait; cancel
CONFIRMEDThe committed planAll required holds committed (BKG-029)Execution observed, or cancellationView, cancel, request help
IN_SERVICETrip under wayMission execution observedOutcome confirmed, or cancellation / recoveryTrack, request help
COMPLETEDTrip ended with outcomeActuals and passenger outcome recorded (SVC-038)TerminalView outcome and refund status
CANCELLEDBooking ended without completionCancellation with reason and capacity release (SVC-038)TerminalView reason and refund status
UNKNOWNThe outcome of the last action is not yet knownTimeout or lost acknowledgementQuery and reconcile establish the actual stateView; request help; not repeat the action

UNKNOWN. UNKNOWN is a knowledge state, not a booking outcome (D04.2); the same distinction applies to the observer's UNKNOWN (ASM-023). It is never resolved by assumption: not to CONFIRMED (which could promise capacity that was not committed) and not to CANCELLED (which could release capacity that was). Only query and reconcile resolve it, and no side effect is duplicated (SVC-039). The app therefore does not offer a "try again" that would submit a second commit; it shows that the outcome is being confirmed and offers help.

Offer expiry. After expiresAt the shown offer can no longer be accepted; a new quote is needed. Expiry of a quote does not release capacity that is already PENDING (BKG-025).

Revision conflict. If the booking or resource revision changed after the terms were shown, acceptance is rejected and the terms are refreshed before any further acceptance (SVC-040). The user sees the refreshed terms beside the original plan.

Stale evidence. If capacity or status evidence is older than its freshness budget, the offer or action is blocked and the reason is shown (SVC-041); the budget is set at G2 (TBD-006).

4.D.7 Operator workspace

The workspace is organised in three columns — capacity and queue, why this offer, permitted action — so that every action is taken with its justification in view (SVC-043). The pairing of each action with its context and guard is in D04.3.

Capacity and queue shows demand by zone and time; reachable vehicles and ready time; seats and cargo space per segment; hub and loading slots and queues; committed trips and spare capacity; cases by severity and dueAt; passenger recovery reserve; cargo custody and failed handovers. It is the operator's basis for deciding to throttle new offers.

Why this offer explains a single offer: the received plan and consent scope; capacity and evidence age; original and inserted route; pickup, arrival and detour impact; discount and freight revenue; dwell, route and handling cost; and, where rejected, the passenger or cargo rejection reason. It shows that the original choice stays accessible to the user.

Permitted actions are executed as domain commands through the owning component, never as direct edits. Each has a precondition; when it does not hold, the action is disabled and the reason is shown.

ActionExecuted byPreconditionRequirement
Recheck all route segmentsC03A route revision existsBKG-004
Protect accepted passenger limitsC03An insertion is proposedBKG-005
Hold seats / cargo / loading slotC03Capacity is feasible on every segmentBKG-034
Confirm terms and custody ownerC02, C06The user has accepted the terms shownBKG-034
Reconcile timeout / lost ACKC02, C03Outcome is unknownSVC-039
Audit each route revisionC03None (read)SVC-017
Release only cleared capacityC03Physical clearance observedBKG-033
Recover each passenger partyC06A case exists with owner and deadlineSVC-013
Own return / failed deliveryC06A failed handover is recordedCAP-086
Throttle infeasible new offersC02, C03No feasible capacity in the zone / timeSVC-042

No operator action can confirm a booking whose holds are not all committed, release capacity whose execution is unknown, or change a user's accepted plan without the user's acceptance. Throttling restricts new offers only; it never withdraws accepted journeys, as in CONSTRAINED mode (CAP-029).

4.D.8 Use cases

UC4.1 Request and accept a plan. Trigger: the user opens the request screen. Main success: (1) user enters the request; (2) app validates and submits the intent; (3) offer screen shows feasible options with expiry; (4) user reviews timing, total price and cancellation terms and accepts; (5) state shows PENDING, then CONFIRMED, and the user can identify the committed plan. Extensions: no feasible capacity — reason shown, no promise; offer expires — new quote required; revision conflict — refreshed terms shown; lost acknowledgement — UNKNOWN shown until reconciled.

UC4.2 Decline a revised offer. Trigger: a time-shift, activity or sharing offer arrives for a confirmed booking. Main success: (1) offer shown beside the original; (2) user declines; (3) original remains CONFIRMED and unchanged. Extension: user ignores the offer — same result at expiry; the refusal or expiry is retained for measurement (SVC-055).

UC4.3 Get help during service. Trigger: the user selects help in the service screen. Main success: (1) a case is opened with an owner and deadline (SVC-020); (2) the user sees the owner; (3) recovery or cancellation is offered; (4) outcome confirmed. Extension: recovery fails — the failure is recorded separately (SVC-045) and the case stays owned.

UC4.4 Explain infeasibility. Trigger: an operator is asked why a request was rejected. Main success: the operator opens "why this offer" and reads the rejection reason, evidence age and segment capacity; the explanation matches the binding reason shown to the user.

UC4.5 Recover a lost acknowledgement. Trigger: a booking shows UNKNOWN in the workspace. Main success: (1) operator selects reconcile; (2) C02 queries the original intent; (3) the actual outcome is recorded; (4) the user sees the resolved state. Postcondition: one booking, one charge. Extension: the outcome stays unknown to its deadline — owned exception with backup owner and fallback (OPS-097).

4.D.9 Failure handling and recovery

ConditionUser appOperator workspacePlatform
No feasible capacityBinding reason; no promiseThrottle new offers in the zone / timeNo hold created
Stale evidenceAction blocked with reasonEvidence age highlightedOffer or action rejected (SVC-041)
Revision conflictRefreshed terms beside originalRoute revision auditAcceptance rejected; terms refreshed
Timeout / lost ACKUNKNOWN; no repeat actionReconcile action enabledQuery and reconcile; no duplicate effect
Cancellation after positioningCANCELLED with reason and refund statusPositioning and recovery owner updatedCapacity released only when cleared
Failed cargo handoverUpdated ETA if the route changesOwn return / failed deliveryFailed handover counted as consumed capacity (CAP-083)

4.D.10 Accessibility, privacy and audit

  • Access needs are first-class request fields and are checked per segment; a sharing or cargo insertion that would remove an accessible position is not offered.
  • Usability results are reported by accessibility need so that a design that works on average but fails for one group is visible (SVC-044).
  • Optional data access is tested as optional: the user can complete the core task with it declined (SVC-004).
  • The workspace shows the consent scope of each received plan, so that an operator can see which information an offer was permitted to use.
  • Every operator action is a domain command with an actor and is auditable; each route revision is auditable from the workspace.

4.D.11 Experiment design: usability tasks and prototype evidence

The concept is tested with a prototype before it is built against live capacity. The test is designed to fail the concept if users misread commitments or operators can create duplicates.

Tasks
Optional data access; keeping the original choice; understanding revised timing; understanding total cost; reaching help; for operators, explaining infeasibility, protecting commitments and recovering a lost acknowledgement.
Conditions
Normal path plus refusal, stale capacity, cancellation after positioning and lost ACK (SVC-044).
Measures
Success, decision time, comprehension, opt-out and acceptance, each by accessibility need; price and timing comprehension; recovery completion; reasons for refusal.
Acceptance
Users identify the committed plan, decline while retaining the original option and reach help; operators explain infeasibility, protect commitments and recover without duplicates (SVC-045).
Recording
Critical errors and failed recovery are recorded separately from task success, so that a high success rate cannot mask a single unsafe outcome.

Participant numbers, task durations and pass levels are not set in the document; they belong with the comparison design reviewed at G2, whose owners are PM, Design and Finance (P07). Prototype acceptance rates are not used as estimates of field acceptance; simulated or prototype acceptance is kept distinct from measured behaviour (SVC-061).

4.D.12 Design rationale and alternatives considered

A short path with detail on demand. Showing every constraint on every screen would make the flow hard to complete; hiding constraints would make offers misleading. The design shows the decision-relevant items (timing, total price, cancellation terms, access compatibility) always and expands detail when the user compares or changes a plan.

Showing UNKNOWN to the user. Hiding uncertainty behind a spinner or optimistic confirmation is common but leads users to repeat actions or to rely on a booking that may not exist. Exposing a distinct state with help available is less polished but prevents duplicates and false promises.

Actions bound to context. A free-form operator console would be more flexible but would allow actions without justification. Pairing each action with its context and guard makes the workspace auditable and makes a blocked action self-explaining.

4.D.13 Open points

  • Freshness budgets that trigger "stale evidence" (TBD-006, decided at G2).
  • Usability sample, task timing and pass levels — not stated; to be set with the comparison design reviewed at G2 (P07).
  • Shared-ride thresholds shown on the offer screen (TBD-029).
  • Response class and escalation behind the help path (TBD-008).

Measurement contract

Service gates apply to each passenger and shipment. Separate booking counts, people, deliveries and vehicle missions. Targets require baseline evidence.

Keep CAPEX and project cash flow distinct.
