5.DDetailed specification

This section specifies the measurement system that decides whether the five mechanisms create value: the counting units and denominators, the north star and the reconciliation that qualifies a journey for it, each measure stated in words with its source records and the failure cases it must retain, the shared-capacity measures for mechanisms 04 and 05, the paired estimate and attribution design, the contribution build used by Finance, the data lineage and missing-data behaviour, and how the measures feed gate decisions.

5.D.1 Purpose and scope

The measures exist to separate real effects from artefacts. Three artefacts are common in mobility services and the measurement contract is designed against each: counting a pooled trip as several trips or as one person; counting a shift or a substituted visit as new demand; and counting a shared cost once per passenger. Every rule in this section prevents one of these.

In scope are the north star, the measure cards, the shared-capacity measures, the paired estimate and the measurement contract (attribution, service and finance). The simulation and field procedures that produce the data are in P06; the gates that consume the results are in P07; the capacity and sharing measures are elaborated in P28–P30.

5.D.2 Actors and responsibilities

Actor / componentResponsibility for measurement
C02Source of requests, offers, acceptances, booking revisions and final request dispositions
C04Source of assignments, arrivals, movement traces and observed boarding, alighting or delivery
C05Source of energy use attributed to missions
Service providersSource of provider actuals (verified visits, observed use)
C07Owns the contract and ledger; reconciles journeys and costs; publishes UsageVerified
PMOwns KPI decisions and the KPI dictionary (SVC-073)
FinanceVerifies revenue scope, cost allocation and investment assumptions
EngineeringOwns trace quality, i.e. that the source records are complete and linkable

5.D.3 Counting units and denominators

Four units are counted separately and never substituted for one another (SVC-047):

Booking
One accepted intent as held by C02. A pooled mission is not counted as one passenger request (CAP-056).
Person
Each passenger within a party. People counts are retained separately from booking counts.
Delivery
Each shipment, counted by its own identity and custody outcome.
Vehicle mission
One mission as recorded by C04, which may carry several intents.

Denominators follow three rules. First, eligibility is decided before the outcome: an "eligible request" or "eligible offer shown" is defined by the request and offer records, not by whether the request was later served. Second, rejected and expired items stay in the denominator: capacity rejects stay in dispatch success, refusals and expired offers stay in conversion and shift acceptance (SVC-055, SVC-056). Third, repeat impressions of the same offer are counted once (SVC-055), so that showing an offer more often cannot lower the denominator's quality.

5.D.4 North star: verified completed journeys

A journey counts only when three independent records reconcile (SVC-046):

  1. Mission evidence from C04 shows that the vehicle mission carrying the intent executed, with observed boarding and alighting (or delivery) for that passenger or shipment.
  2. Service actual from C02 / C07 shows that the booked service — trip, and activity where combined — took place as accepted, or as revised and re-accepted.
  3. User outcome shows the result for the user, including refund status where applicable.

The join uses the traceability key chain of P02 (SVC-016). A journey whose records do not reconcile is not counted and is not discarded: it remains visible as unreconciled until resolved, so that a reconciliation backlog cannot be mistaken for a fall in demand. Assignment alone is never completion (SVC-056). For shared missions each passenger and shipment is evaluated separately; one mission can contribute several verified journeys, and one failed passenger outcome does not invalidate the others.

The north star is deliberately a count of verified service rather than of bookings or revenue, because both of those can rise while service to users falls.

5.D.5 Measures in words

The definitions and sources are tabulated in D05.2. This subsection states, for each group, what each measure is meant to reveal and which cases it must not hide.

01 Positioning. Pickup wait is computed per passenger from the C02 requested pickup time and the C04 actual pickup; negative values (early arrival) count as zero so that early vehicles do not offset late ones. It is reported as median and p95, and late and missed pickups are reported separately because a missed pickup has no actual pickup time and would otherwise vanish from the distribution (SVC-054). Empty travel divides empty vehicle-km by completed trips and includes the travel spent on advance positioning, including positioning that was wasted and return movements; otherwise mechanism 01 would hide its own cost. Dispatch success divides assigned missions by eligible requests, keeping capacity rejects in the denominator. Required fleet is the minimum tested fleet that meets all service gates, found by the fleet sweep of P25–P28 with demand, hubs and service gates held fixed, and reported with its uncertainty (TBD-046).

02 New demand. Offer conversion divides accepted activity offers by eligible offers shown, with repeat impressions deduplicated. Additional trips is the difference in completed trips between treatment and matched baseline; the net change includes displaced use, so substitution of trips the user would have made anyway is identified rather than counted as new. Fleet utilization divides productive by available hours and also reports scheduled hours; the scope of "productive" is stated explicitly because including positioning or waiting would change the result. Activity use counts verified additional provider visits from provider actuals, keeping gross and net use separate and keeping visits separate from user spending.

03 Smoothing. Shift acceptance divides accepted time changes by eligible shift offers shown, retaining refusals and expired offers. Peak demand counts requests per fixed interval before and after accepted shifts, using original and revised request times; the interval width is fixed across all runs because changing it can create or remove an apparent peak. Unserved demand divides unserved eligible requests by all eligible requests by zone and time, using the final request disposition, and shows cause, zone and peak interval. Promise kept divides on-time pickups by pickups due, including missed pickups, against the accepted window; it also reports how often the window itself was changed, so that a shift that moves the promise is not counted as a promise kept.

Net economics. Net revenue is recognized revenue after discounts and refunds, counted once, with operator and provider scope kept distinct. Incremental cost is extra travel, energy, service and app operating cost from C04, C05 and the cost ledger, including added support and refunds. Incremental contribution is the change in recognized revenue less the change in attributable cost between matched arms, reported both in total and per completed trip, with app cost included once and its allocation documented. Interaction effect is the combined gain less the sum of the separately tested gains; it reports overlap and capacity effects and is meaningful only when all gains share one baseline and one unit.

5.D.6 Shared-capacity measures (04 / 05)

Sharing changes the relation between passengers, missions and costs, so mechanisms 04 and 05 have their own measures: passenger journeys per vehicle-hour; seat-km utilization; detour; freight delivery and lateness; cargo dwell; and displaced passenger trips. Their purpose is to show passenger output, freight delivery and net contribution together, so that a gain in one cannot be reported without the loss it causes in another.

  • Detour is measured per passenger against the limit that passenger accepted (SVC-009), not as a fleet average.
  • Cargo dwell and failed handovers are counted as consumed capacity (CAP-083).
  • Displaced passenger trips are retained as unserved demand, not dropped from the denominator.
  • Shared-ride evidence shows total contribution and passenger fulfilment together (CAP-077).

Detailed definitions and failure cases: P29 22.3–22.4, P30 23.3–23.4.

5.D.7 Paired estimate and uncertainty

Every effect is reported as the paired estimate (SVC-053):

ΔK = K_effect − K_baseline

Pairing means that K_effect and K_baseline are computed on runs that share initial conditions, seeds, demand trace, faults, fleet and hubs, accounting basis and cost boundary (SVC-057). The estimate is reported with the distribution of differences across repeated runs and its uncertainty, not as a single value. Where a measure is a ratio, both numerator and denominator are taken from the same paired runs. A difference that is within run-to-run variation is reported as such; it is not rounded into a gain.

5.D.8 Experiment design: attribution

Attribution separates five sources of change: additional demand, time shifts, substitution, pooled passengers and delivered shipments (SVC-049). The design proceeds in a fixed order (D05.3):

  1. Baseline with all effects off on the same fleet, hubs, demand and faults.
  2. Isolated effects 01–03, each compared with matched inputs.
  3. Four conditions for 04 / 05 — single-party, shared rides, passenger + cargo, combined — with effects 01–03 held fixed (SVC-050, CAP-090).
  4. Interactions, measured as the interaction effect against the sum of separately tested gains.

For a shared route, the route has several intents but one vehicle mission, so route distance and common costs are counted once and then allocated; they are never summed across intents. Field validation of these effects follows the field design of P06, where spillover across users and zones is checked (TBD-030).

5.D.9 Finance: contribution build

The contribution is built in one direction so that nothing is counted twice (SVC-052):

  1. Start from net passenger fares. These already reflect sharing discounts and displaced trips; no separate discount line is deducted again.
  2. Add recognized freight revenue.
  3. Deduct route, handling, energy, support, cleaning, recovery, returns and app costs, each once.
  4. Show total contribution alongside unit measures.

CAPEX and project cash flow are kept distinct from operating contribution (CAP-065); a positive operating contribution is therefore not a statement of project profitability, which operational feasibility does not by itself establish either (ASM-032). Contribution weights and versioned deductions used in settlement are governed by the contract revision (TBD-034); the finance record content is in P07 (SVC-072).

5.D.10 Rules and invariants

  1. R5.1 A journey counts toward the north star only when mission evidence, service actual and user outcome reconcile (SVC-046).
  2. R5.2 Bookings, people, deliveries and vehicle missions are counted separately; service gates apply per passenger and per shipment (SVC-047).
  3. R5.3 A target is set only with baseline evidence (SVC-048).
  4. R5.4 Route distance and common costs of a shared route are counted once (SVC-049).
  5. R5.5 Unserved passenger and cargo requests are retained, and passenger and freight fulfilment are reported separately (SVC-051).
  6. R5.6 Refusals, expired offers and capacity rejects stay in their denominators; repeat impressions are deduplicated (SVC-055, SVC-056).
  7. R5.7 Every effect is a paired estimate with repeated-run differences and uncertainty (SVC-053).
  8. R5.8 Gains being combined share one baseline and one unit.
  9. R5.9 A gain fails when realistic costs erase contribution or any accepted service limit breaks (SVC-059).

5.D.11 Data and lineage

Each measure is computed from source records, never from another derived measure unless that dependency is stated (D05.1). The source records are written by one component each (PLT-009) and delivered by events — BookingChanged, AllocationCommitted, MissionObserved, EnergyUpdated, UsageVerified — through the idempotent inbox, so that redelivery does not double-count (PLT-015). Replay for recomputation uses separate projections and produces no external effect (PLT-017).

Missing data. A record that is missing is not imputed as success or failure. The journey remains unreconciled and is reported in a separate count, and the missing-data behaviour is part of what must reconcile at pilot exit (SVC-027). Corrections in settlement carry correction links over I08 (I08) so that a corrected value can be traced to the original.

Provenance. Each reported value carries the scenario or pilot it came from, its run identity and its effect switches, as defined for the reproducible evidence record (SVC-060).

5.D.12 Decision process

Measures inform gates but do not pass them on their own. At G2 the KPI dictionary and comparison design are agreed; at G3 the KPI baseline must reconcile; at G4 effect ranges, adverse outcomes, full costs and counter-evidence are reviewed; at G5 second-site results are compared on the same measures (P07). Service feasibility and customer choice remain binding even when aggregate contribution improves (SVC-075): a mechanism that raises incremental contribution while breaking promise kept, detour limits or unserved-demand guardrails does not advance.

5.D.13 Verification approach

  • Definition review: each measure is inspected against its card — numerator, denominator, source, reporting rule — before any run (D05.2).
  • Counting tests: synthetic traces with a pooled mission, a mission with cargo, a missed pickup, a refused offer, a repeat impression and an expired offer, each checked for correct counts in every affected measure.
  • Ledger tests: a shared mission is checked for costs counted once and revenue counted once across passenger and freight lines (SVC-014).
  • Pairing tests: baseline and treatment runs are checked for identical seeds, demand traces and cost boundaries before their difference is accepted (SVC-057).

5.D.14 Design rationale and alternatives considered

Verified journeys rather than bookings as the north star. Bookings can rise through repeated offers, revenue through price, and utilization through positioning. A verified journey requires both service and evidence, and is chosen because it cannot rise while the user is served worse.

Paired estimates rather than before / after comparison. A before / after comparison would confound mechanism effects with demand changes, season and fleet changes. Paired runs remove those differences by construction; in the field, the comparison arm serves the same purpose.

Four conditions before interactions. Testing all five effects together would be faster but would make it impossible to tell whether a combined gain is real or an overlap of two effects claiming the same capacity. Isolating 04 and 05 in four conditions with 01–03 held fixed allows the interaction effect to be measured as a residual.

One-direction contribution build. Starting from net fares that already include sharing discounts avoids the common error of deducting a discount from a fare that was already discounted.

5.D.15 Open points

  • KPI targets — require baseline evidence (TBD-031).
  • Required fleet — set by the fleet sweep (TBD-046).
  • Fixed interval width for peak demand and the scope of productive hours — to be stated in the KPI dictionary agreed at G2 (P07).
  • Contribution weights and versioned deductions (TBD-034).
  • Field assignment unit, observation window and thresholds (TBD-030).
  • Cost boundaries for passenger and freight gates — agreed at G2 (TBD-050).

Mobility service planning / Product management supplementP06 / 30

Controlled experiments and evidence workflow

Simulation tests five mechanisms under stated assumptions. Field trials measure actual acceptance, shared-route performance and handling time.

06Discovery & validation

Evidence loopObserve demand and choices / calibrate assumptions / repeat comparisons / approve the next bounded test

D06.1SequenceEvidence workflow from observation to a recorded decision

Experiment design / Attribution and interaction

  1. Baseline

  2. Isolated effects

Stress tests

Sweep lead time, forecast error, acceptance, substitution and discounts. Vary route overlap, party size, allowed detour, cargo mass / volume, handling time and delivery windows. Test peak demand, hub loss, no-shows, absent recipients and vehicle recovery. Preserve passenger / shipment identity. Reject future-information leakage. Gains fail when realistic costs erase contribution or any accepted service limit breaks.

Proposed tests only. Simulation outputs do not establish field impact or guarantee service-level attainment.

Reproducible evidence record

Record engine / scenario version, input units / sources, demand trace, information receipt times, initial fleet / hub state, seed and effect switches. Retain offer / intent linkage, acceptance, original / revised time, trip / activity actuals, rejected demand and ledger entries. Report paired differences and uncertainty across repeated runs.
Field design: predefine assignment unit, observation window and thresholds. Shared vehicles create spillover across users and zones. Check non-participation, displacement and rebound demand. Keep simulated acceptance distinct from measured behavior.
Decision packet: input provenance, reproducible run, outcome distribution, guardrail failures, sensitivity, accountable owner and a documented continue / revise / stop decision. Unsupported effects stay unvalidated.

D06.2Decision logicWhen a measured gain fails or stays unvalidated

Checks applied to a paired comparison before it can enter the decision packet. A run that leaks future information or loses passenger / shipment identity is rejected; a gain that breaks a service limit or is erased by realistic costs fails.

Source: P06 stress tests; P06 reproducible evidence record; P06 experiment design

6.DDetailed specification

This section specifies the evidence workflow behind the five value mechanisms: who frames and runs a test, how paired simulation runs and stress sweeps are designed, how a bounded field check is set up and guarded, which record each run must leave, and how a documented continue / revise / stop decision is reached. It turns the loop drawn in 06 and the attribution design below it into use cases, rules and verification steps that a product, engineering and operations team can execute and audit.

6.D.1 Purpose and scope

The workflow exists so that every claim about a mechanism — advance positioning, additional demand, demand smoothing, shared rides and passenger–freight sharing (P01) — is backed by a reproducible comparison against a matched baseline and, before any expansion, by measured field behaviour. Simulation is used to test mechanisms under stated assumptions; the bounded pilot is used to measure what simulation cannot: actual acceptance, shared-route performance and handling time. The two are kept as different kinds of evidence throughout.

In scope: framing a mechanism for test, paired simulation runs, isolated and combined effect comparisons, stress sweeps, the reproducible evidence record, the field design of a bounded pilot, and the decision packet handed to the accountable owner. Out of scope: the measure formulas themselves, which are defined in P05; the gate sequence that consumes the decision packets, defined in P07; and the system tests of contracts and fault paths, defined in P24. All tests described here are proposed; none has been run (ASM-029).

6.D.2 Users and scenarios

The workflow has internal users. Each needs a different answer from the same evidence:

PM
Needs to know whether a mechanism improves user outcomes under realistic acceptance, so that scope and KPI decisions are not taken on optimistic assumptions.
Operations
Needs to know whether the service stays inside capacity and recovery limits when the mechanism is switched on — queues, recovery load, hub occupancy and support coverage.
Finance
Needs a net contribution in which shared costs are counted once and the cost boundary is the same in every arm, so that a gain is not created by moving cost outside the comparison.
Design
Needs measured comprehension and refusal behaviour from the field, which simulation can only assume.
Engineering
Needs runs that can be repeated exactly from the record, and trace quality sufficient to link offers, acceptances and actuals.

Typical scenarios:

  1. New mechanism framing. Observation shows that residents with a known free-time interval rarely book a reachable activity. Mechanism 02 is framed with its input, action, test measure, limit, outcome and failure condition before any run (SVC-006).
  2. Interaction question. Shared rides (04) and passenger–freight sharing (05) each show a gain alone. The team needs to know whether the combined gain is smaller than the sum because both consume the same seat-km and dwell time.
  3. Fragility question. A smoothing gain (03) looks robust at the assumed acceptance. The team needs to know at what acceptance, discount or forecast error the gain disappears or a service limit breaks.
  4. Field confirmation. A simulated gain has survived the stress sweep. A bounded pilot must measure actual sharing acceptance, detour, wait and cargo dwell without letting spillover between users and zones contaminate the comparison.

6.D.3 Actors and responsibilities

ActorResponsibility in the workflowProduces
PMFrames the mechanism; owns user outcomes, scope and KPI decisions; normally the accountable owner of the decision (SVC-073)Mechanism definition; decision
DesignSpecifies how original and alternative offers are shown and refused; owns comprehension and accessibility evidenceOffer variants; usability evidence (P04)
EngineeringMaintains the engine / scenario version, run reproducibility and trace quality; rejects invalid runsReproducible evidence record
Operations / partnersConfirms fleet / hub capacity and fault assumptions; staffs recovery in the pilot; applies stop / rollback rulesCapacity inputs; field actuals
FinanceFixes the accounting basis and cost boundary; verifies that each cost is counted onceCost ledger basis; net contribution check

The person who runs a comparison does not decide on it alone: the decision packet is closed by the accountable owner, and every HOLD that follows names a closure owner (SVC-074).

6.D.4 Use cases

UC6.1 Frame a mechanism for test. Goal: a mechanism is testable and falsifiable before any evidence is gathered. Trigger: an observation from the OBSERVE step (lead time, free time, price sensitivity, alternatives) suggests a mechanism. Main success scenario:

  1. PM separates measured inputs (with their source and units) from assumptions (with their stated range or TBD status).
  2. PM records the mechanism's input, action, test measure, limit, outcome and failure condition (SVC-006).
  3. Finance confirms the accounting basis and cost boundary that every arm will use.
  4. Operations confirms the fleet / hub capacity and fault set to be held fixed.
  5. The frame is recorded as the scenario definition referenced by every run.

Extensions: At step 1, an input cannot be sourced: it stays an assumption and is swept in the stress tests rather than fixed. At step 2, no failure condition can be stated: the mechanism is not evaluated; it returns to OBSERVE.

UC6.2 Run a paired comparison. Goal: an effect estimate that differs from baseline only by the effect switch. Trigger: a framed mechanism. Main success scenario:

  1. Engineering fixes the engine / scenario version, demand / outage trace, initial fleet / hub state and seeds.
  2. The baseline arm runs with all effects off; each effect arm runs with the same inputs and seeds and only its switch changed (SVC-057).
  3. Runs repeat across seeds; the paired difference is computed per seed and reported with its uncertainty (SVC-053).
  4. The evidence record is written for every run (SVC-060).

Extensions: At step 2, a run reads information whose receipt time is after the decision time: the run is rejected (SVC-003). At step 2, a passenger or shipment loses its identity across a shared route or revised offer: the run is rejected (SVC-011). At step 3, the uncertainty spans zero: the effect stays unvalidated.

UC6.3 Stress the gain. Goal: the limits at which a gain fails are known. Trigger: an effect with a paired estimate. Main success scenario: the sweep varies lead time, forecast error, acceptance, substitution and discounts; route overlap, party size, allowed detour, cargo mass / volume, handling time and delivery windows; and adds peak demand, hub loss, no-shows, absent recipients and vehicle recovery (SVC-058). Each sweep point is itself a paired comparison. Extension: at any point where realistic costs erase contribution or an accepted service limit breaks, the gain is recorded as failed at that point (SVC-059).

UC6.4 Run a bounded field check. Goal: measured acceptance and service outcomes for an effect that has survived UC6.3. Trigger: approval of the next bounded test. Main success scenario:

  1. The field design predefines the assignment unit, the observation window and the thresholds before any participant is exposed (SVC-061, TBD-030).
  2. Stop / rollback rules and the staffed recovery path are agreed with Operations.
  3. The pilot measures sharing acceptance, actual detour / wait, cargo dwell / delivery and net service and cost.
  4. Spillover, non-participation, displacement and rebound demand are checked and reported.

Extensions: At step 3, a stop / rollback rule fires: exposure ends, affected journeys are recovered by the owner of passenger recovery and cargo exceptions (SVC-013), and the decision packet records the guardrail failure. At step 4, spillover between arms cannot be bounded with the chosen assignment unit: the field estimate is reported as contaminated and the effect stays unvalidated.

UC6.5 Compile and close the decision packet. Goal: a documented continue / revise / stop decision. Main success scenario: the packet assembles input provenance, the reproducible run, the outcome distribution, guardrail failures, sensitivity and the accountable owner; the owner records the decision (SVC-062). Extension: the owner cannot decide on the evidence presented — the packet is returned with the missing evidence named, and the gate holds (P07).

6.D.5 Experiment design

The comparison order is fixed and each stage depends on the previous one being valid (see D06.1):

StageWhat variesWhat is held fixedQuestion answered
BaselineNothing; all effects offFleet / hubs, demand and faults, demand / outage trace, accounting basis, cost boundaryReference outcome for every paired difference
Isolated effectsOne effect switch at a time: 01, 02 or 03 alone; pooling only; cargo onlyAll shared inputs and seeds of the baselineGain attributable to one mechanism
Combined effectsPooling and cargo together across the four conditions, with 01–03 held fixed; then all five effectsSame as baseline; cost counted onceInteraction, including capacity interaction
Field checkExposure of the assignment unitPredefined window and thresholdsActual acceptance and service outcomes

The four conditions for 04 / 05 are single-party (no pooling / cargo), shared rides (pooling only), passenger + cargo (cargo only) and combined (pooling + cargo), which is the minimum set that separates two effects from their interaction (SVC-050). Effects 01–03 are held fixed during that step because they change the demand that pooling and cargo act on; varying them at the same time would confound the interaction estimate. Only after the pooling–cargo interaction is understood are all five effects combined.

Shared vehicles mean that users are not independent: one user's acceptance of a shared ride changes the detour and seat availability of others in the same zone. The field design therefore chooses the assignment unit so that the comparison can be read despite this spillover, and states the choice before the test. The unit, window and thresholds are not fixed in this document; they are predefined before the field test (TBD-030).

6.D.6 Measures

The measures are those of P05; this workflow fixes how they are compared.

Paired estimate
For an outcome K, the difference between the effect arm and the baseline arm run on the same seed and inputs, collected across repeated runs and reported with its uncertainty, not as a single value (SVC-053).
Interaction
The combined gain minus the sum of the separately tested gains, measured on one baseline and in one unit; overlap and capacity effects are reported, not netted away.
Run outputs
Request outcome, pickup delay, empty km, activity use, queues, recovery load and net contribution, each traceable to the request and ledger entries in the record.
Field outcomes
Sharing acceptance, actual detour / wait, cargo dwell / delivery and net service and cost, kept distinct from the simulated acceptance that produced the prior estimate.
Failure
A gain fails at a sweep point when realistic costs erase contribution or any accepted service limit breaks; the point and the limit are recorded.

Rejected demand, refusals and expired offers are part of every arm's outcome. Excluding them would make an arm that rejects more demand look more efficient (SVC-051, SVC-055).

6.D.7 Rules and invariants

  1. R6.1 A mechanism is evaluated only after its input, action, test measure, limit, outcome and failure condition are recorded (SVC-006).
  2. R6.2 Paired runs share initial conditions and random seeds, and every arm shares fleet / hubs, demand, faults, accounting basis and cost boundary with the baseline (SVC-057).
  3. R6.3 No decision in a run may use information whose recorded receipt time is later than the decision time; a run that does is rejected, not corrected (SVC-003).
  4. R6.4 Passenger and shipment identity is preserved across shared routes and revised offers in every run (SVC-011).
  5. R6.5 Each effect has its own control switch; independent controls are retained for all five effects even after a combined result is accepted (SVC-030).
  6. R6.6 Route distance and common costs of a shared route are counted once in every arm (SVC-049, SVC-014).
  7. R6.7 A gain is recorded as failed when realistic costs erase contribution or any accepted service limit breaks (SVC-059).
  8. R6.8 The field assignment unit, observation window and thresholds are predefined; simulated acceptance is never reported as measured behaviour (SVC-061).
  9. R6.9 An effect with no supporting evidence stays unvalidated; absence of failure is not evidence of gain (SVC-062).
  10. R6.10 Service feasibility and customer choice remain binding when aggregate contribution improves: a gain that requires breaking an accepted limit is not a gain (SVC-075).

6.D.8 Data and state

The evidence record (D06.3) is written per run and is append-only: a corrected input produces a new run with a new record, never an edit of an old one. The groups are used as follows.

  • Run identity — engine / scenario version, seed and effect switches — is what makes a run repeatable; two runs are a valid pair only if their identities differ in effect switches alone.
  • Inputs carry units and sources so that a reviewer can tell a measured input from an assumption. Information receipt times are recorded so that R6.3 can be checked mechanically rather than by inspection.
  • Retained outcomes link each offer to its intent and acceptance, the original and revised time, trip / activity actuals, rejected demand and ledger entries. The same traceability contract as the product (SVC-016, SVC-017) is applied in simulation, so that a simulated journey and a field journey can be read with one dictionary.
  • Reporting holds paired differences and their uncertainty across repeated runs; individual run outcomes are retained, not only summaries.
  • Field design is written before exposure and is immutable once the pilot starts; a change of design starts a new field check.
  • Decision packet references the records above by run identity rather than copying values, so the outcome distribution shown to the owner is always reproducible from its source.

An effect moves through three standings in this workflow: unvalidated (the default), supported in simulation, and measured in the field. A failure at a stress point or a guardrail failure in the field is recorded against the standing it was found in; the standing does not advance while a failure stands unexplained.

6.D.9 Failure handling and recovery

FailureDetected byHandling
Future-information leakageReceipt time later than decision time in the recordReject the run; fix the scenario; rerun the whole pair (D06.2)
Identity lostIntent with no linked actual, or two intents mergedReject the run; correct the identity handling before any further comparison
Arms not matchedRun identities differ in more than effect switchesPair invalid; results are not reported as an effect
Service limit breaksGuardrail check on run or field outcomesGain fails at that point; record guardrail failure and adverse outcomes
Costs erase contributionNet contribution on the fixed cost boundaryGain fails; record the cost lines that erased it
Pilot guardrail firesStop / rollback rules in the field checkEnd exposure; recover affected journeys through the named owner; record in the packet
Missing field dataGaps against the predefined observation windowReport the gap; do not impute acceptance from simulation

Recovery of a failed experiment is always a new run or a new field check, never a re-labelling of the old one. This keeps the record usable as counter-evidence at G4, where adverse outcomes and counter-evidence are required inputs (P07).

6.D.10 Security, privacy and audit

Field observation and the bounded pilot use consented signals only, each with an explicit purpose, expiry and withdrawal path (SVC-001). Opting out of a pilot leaves the user with the original service; consent is never forced and optional data access stays optional (SVC-004), and a suggestion takes effect only after explicit acceptance (SVC-005). Non-participation is itself a measured outcome, so a design that pressures participation would also bias the result.

Demand traces derived from real journeys are inputs to simulation and carry their source and consent scope in the record. The audit trail of a decision is the decision packet plus the referenced run records; together they let a reviewer re-run the comparison and see the same distribution, guardrail failures and sensitivity that the owner saw.

6.D.11 Decision process

  1. The packet is complete only when it contains input provenance, a reproducible run, the outcome distribution, guardrail failures, sensitivity and the accountable owner (SVC-062).
  2. Continue approves the next bounded test — a wider sweep, a field check, or a gate review — within a stated scope.
  3. Revise changes the mechanism, offer or field design; the revision starts at FRAME, and the earlier records remain as evidence.
  4. Stop ends the mechanism's evaluation; its independent control stays off and the reason is recorded.
  5. New evidence from any outcome is fed back to calibrate assumptions in the next pass of the loop.

The packets feed the gates: framing and comparison design are G2 evidence, the combined-effect comparison and field outcomes are G4 evidence, and the second-site repetition is G5 evidence (D07.3). A packet never passes a gate on its own; the gate review applies its own HOLD conditions.

6.D.12 Verification approach

The workflow itself is verified, not only the mechanisms it tests:

  • Reproducibility check — re-running a recorded run from its identity and inputs gives the same outcomes; a mismatch invalidates every pair that uses that run.
  • Null check — a pair whose effect switch is off in both arms shows no difference beyond its uncertainty; a difference indicates that something other than the switch varies.
  • Leakage check — an injected scenario in which information arrives after a decision is rejected by the run validity check.
  • Identity check — a shared route with several intents and a revised offer keeps one record per passenger and shipment, linked to one vehicle mission (SVC-012).
  • Cost check — the cost of one shared mission appears once in the ledger entries of a combined arm.
  • Packet check — a review confirms each packet field is present and references a stored record before the owner decides.

6.D.13 Design rationale and alternatives considered

Paired runs rather than independent runs. Independent random runs would need many more repetitions to separate a mechanism's effect from demand noise; pairing on seed and inputs removes the shared noise and leaves the effect. The cost is the discipline of holding every other input fixed, which the run identity enforces.

Baseline, isolated, then combined. Starting with all effects on would show a total but not where it comes from, and would hide a mechanism that subtracts value. The fixed order makes attribution possible and exposes capacity interactions between pooling and cargo.

Stress sweep before field. A field check is expensive and exposes real users; the sweep locates the conditions under which a gain fails so that the field design can target them and set stop rules. Simulation alone was rejected as sufficient because acceptance, detour tolerance and handling time are behaviours, not parameters.

Gains fail on costs or limits. An alternative would be to report gross gains and treat costs separately. That would allow a mechanism to look positive while making the service worse or the economics negative; making both conditions part of the failure definition keeps service feasibility and net value binding.

6.D.14 Open points

  • Field design: assignment unit, observation window and thresholds — predefined before the field test (TBD-030).
  • KPI targets require baseline evidence and are not set by this workflow (TBD-031).
  • Required fleet is found by the fleet sweep of P25–P28 (TBD-046).
  • Shared-ride thresholds and operating authority are agreed before pilot release (TBD-029).

    Schedule alone never passes a gate. HOLD for unresolved safety / privacy / legal risk, unknown execution, missing evidence, unstaffed support, partner unreadiness, unreliable data or unreconciled cost.

PM owns user outcomes, scope and KPI decisions. Design owns comprehension and accessibility. Engineering owns contracts, trace quality and release. Operations / partners own service capacity and recovery. Finance verifies revenue scope, cost allocation and investment assumptions. Every HOLD has a named closure owner.

7.DDetailed specification

This section specifies how the release and scale gates G1–G5 operate as an evidence-driven decision process: what each gate requires on entry and on exit, how a review reaches GO, HOLD or REVISE, how a failed condition sends scope back to an earlier gate, what the GO / HOLD and finance records must contain, and how the process itself is audited. It complements the gate state machine (D07.1), the record model (D07.2) and the evidence matrix (D07.3).

7.D.1 Purpose and scope

The gates control the growth of exposure: who uses the service, where, with which mechanisms and at what operating scale. Each gate asks whether the evidence for customer response, operating feasibility and net value is strong enough to justify the next increment of exposure, and whether the organisation can run and recover that increment. Gates are evidence checkpoints, not calendar phases (ASM-027); a planned date is an input to scheduling the review, never a reason to pass it (SVC-063).

In scope: the gate review procedure, entry and exit evidence per gate, the HOLD / REVISE / return rules, decision ownership, the GO / HOLD record and the finance record. Out of scope: how the evidence is produced (experiments in P06, measures in P05, system verification in P24) and the MVP entry and exit conditions themselves (P03), which the gates consume.

7.D.2 Users and scenarios

  • Gate owner preparing a review. The owners named for a gate assemble the evidence, check it against the gate's check, and propose an outcome. They need to know in advance which evidence is mandatory so that a review is not convened on an incomplete packet.
  • Reviewer challenging a GO. A reviewer from another discipline — for example Finance at G4 — needs to see the baseline, the observed KPI and the counter-evidence in one record, and to be able to block on unreconciled cost even when service outcomes look good.
  • Site owner at expansion. At G5 the rollout lead and site owner need to show that local demand, provider capacity and costs at a second site do not invalidate the first site's conclusions.
  • Owner of a HOLD. The named closure owner needs a precise statement of the gap, the evidence that would close it, the deadline and the scope restriction that applies until then.

7.D.3 Actors and responsibilities

ActorDecision rightsGates where named owner
PMUser outcomes, scope and KPI decisionsG1, G2, G4
DesignComprehension and accessibilityG2
EngineeringContracts, trace quality and releaseG3
Operations / partnersService capacity and recoveryG1, G3, G4
FinanceVerifies revenue scope, cost allocation and investment assumptionsG2, G4
Rollout lead + site ownerSecond-site repetition and local limitsG5

Ownership is by decision type, not by gate (SVC-073). A discipline that is not a named owner of a gate can still raise a HOLD condition within its decision rights: Engineering can hold a G4 review on trace quality, and Finance can hold any gate on unreconciled cost. Every HOLD names its closure owner (SVC-074).

7.D.4 Preconditions and inputs

A gate review may be convened only when the following hold; otherwise the review is postponed rather than held with a predictable HOLD outcome.

  1. The previous gate has a recorded GO for the same user segment / site, or the review is a re-entry after a recorded return.
  2. The gate's evidence items are present as records, not as summaries: for G2 the causal model, offer tests, KPI dictionary and comparison design; for G4 the effect range, adverse outcomes, full costs and counter-evidence; and so on per D07.3.
  3. Experimental evidence is presented as decision packets with input provenance and reproducible runs (SVC-062).
  4. Open items that the gate must decide are listed with their current state — at G2, for example, the constraint register entries (SVC-032) and the platform decisions on hosting zones, failover, protocols, recovery objectives, latency and freshness budgets (PLT-025).

7.D.5 Gate entry and exit criteria

The table expands each gate's purpose into what must be true to enter, what is decided, and where a failed condition typically returns.

GateEnters withDecidesExit evidence (summary)Typical return target on failure
G1 DISCOVERA candidate user problemWhich users, zones and time windows are studied (TBD-049)Journey / demand map with request denominators; traceable service and cost baselines; sampling gaps and consent boundaries recorded—
G2 DEFINEG1 baselinesMechanism definitions and controls; passenger and freight gates; cost boundaries; consent, capacity and custody ownership (TBD-050)Causal model, offer tests, KPI dictionary, comparison design; constraint register with TBDs explicitG1 if the user problem or baseline is invalidated
G3 PILOT READYG2 definitions and constraint registerWhether the system and organisation can run and recover the bounded pilotC01–C07 normal and fault paths passed; segment limits, route revisions, no duplicate intents, auditable costs; rehearsed no-show, failed delivery and rollback (SVC-068)G2 if a constraint or ownership assumption is invalidated
G4 LEARNA running bounded pilotWhich mechanisms continue, under which limitsIndividual and combined effects with matched inputs; sharing acceptance, detour, handling time; displaced trips and failed deliveries retained; net contribution under realistic conditionsG3 for an operational fault path; G2 for an invalid causal model
G5 REPEATG4 GO at the first siteExpansion within a verified operating envelope (SVC-069)Second-site results, support cost, sensitivity, partner acceptance; packaged configuration, training, monitoring and recoveryG4 if gains do not survive weak acceptance or supply loss; G2 if local limits change the service boundary

The G3 technical evidence is the system design chapters: reservation and service contracts in P08–P11, fault injection and release dependencies in P24, capacity and recovery in P25–P28, and sharing rules in P29–P30. G3 evidence is recorded per case with scenario / ODD slice, initial state, revisions, injected fault, trace and oracle result, as stated in P24 17.3; G4 uses observed outcomes and G5 adds repeatable onboarding.

7.D.6 Behaviour

Main flow — gate review.

  1. The named owners confirm the preconditions in 7.D.4 and circulate the evidence.
  2. Each evidence item is checked against the gate's check (for example, at G1, missing demand and selection bias; at G4, whether the net gain survives realistic response).
  3. Every HOLD condition is tested explicitly: unresolved safety / privacy / legal risk, unknown execution, missing evidence, unstaffed support, partner unreadiness, unreliable data, unreconciled cost (SVC-064). The result of each test is recorded, including "not present".
  4. If no HOLD condition is present and the GO preconditions hold — named service owner, trained operation, support coverage, data quality and rollback path (SVC-071) — the outcome is GO for the stated segment / site and scope.
  5. The GO / HOLD record is written with all required fields (SVC-070) and, where finance is in scope, the finance record (SVC-072).
  6. Scope expands only after the record is written.

Alternative flow — REVISE. When the evidence shows that the proposal can pass with a defined change, the outcome is REVISE. The record names an owner, the required evidence, a deadline and a temporary scope restriction, and records the rollback trigger and the resume authority (SVC-065). Scope runs restricted until the owner returns with the evidence and the review records a new outcome.

Alternative flow — HOLD. When any HOLD condition is present, scope stays where it is or is reduced. The closure owner, the gap and the next review trigger are recorded. HOLD differs from REVISE in that the way forward is not yet known: the owner must first establish what evidence would close the gap.

Exception flow — return to an earlier gate.

  1. A failed condition is traced to the assumption it invalidates (user problem, mechanism definition, constraint, ownership, operational path, economics).
  2. The earliest gate whose evidence depends on that assumption is identified (SVC-066).
  3. All later GO records that depend on the assumption are marked as no longer current; exposure granted by them is held.
  4. The named owner closes the evidence gap at the earliest gate; the review then proceeds forward again through every intervening gate.

Exception flow — triggered rollback. When a recorded rollback trigger fires during a pilot or rollout, the rollback path named in the GO record is executed, affected passengers and shipments are recovered by their owners, and the gate re-enters review in HOLD. Resumption requires the recorded resume authority.

7.D.7 Rules and invariants

  1. R7.1 Schedule alone never passes a gate (SVC-063).
  2. R7.2 Any HOLD condition present at review produces HOLD, regardless of other results (SVC-064).
  3. R7.3 GO requires all GO preconditions; a missing rollback path or uncovered support is a HOLD, not a GO with a note (SVC-071).
  4. R7.4 A failed condition returns to the earliest invalidated gate, and scope stays held until the named owner closes the gap and the decision is recorded (SVC-066).
  5. R7.5 Every REVISE carries owner, required evidence, deadline, temporary scope restriction, rollback trigger and resume authority (SVC-065).
  6. R7.6 Every HOLD has a named closure owner (SVC-074).
  7. R7.7 Consent, capacity and custody ownership are agreed at G2 before any evaluation uses them (SVC-067).
  8. R7.8 Service feasibility and customer choice remain binding even when aggregate contribution improves (SVC-075, ASM-028).
  9. R7.9 Expansion at G5 is approved only within a verified operating envelope; a configuration qualifies only within its tested demand, geography and operating conditions (SVC-069, ASM-031).
  10. R7.10 Targets that a gate compares against are set only with baseline evidence (SVC-048).

7.D.8 Data and state

Each gate, for each user segment / site, has one current outcome from the set GO, HOLD, REVISE (D07.1). Records are append-only: a new review writes a new GO / HOLD record that supersedes the previous one; earlier records remain for audit. A record's fields are grouped as in D07.2:

Decision
Decision + date and user segment / site identify what was decided and for which exposure. The date records when the evidence was judged, not when the gate was planned.
Evidence
Baseline and observed KPI, and the acceptance trace, link the decision to the measures of P05 and the decision packets of P06. The baseline is the one used for target setting.
Open risk
Unresolved safety / legal / operational risk and the scope restriction that bounds it. A GO may carry residual risk only if it is stated and does not meet a HOLD condition.
Follow-up
Accountable owner and next review trigger. The trigger is an evidence event (for example, an exposure milestone, a guardrail breach, a partner change), consistent with gates not being calendar phases.
Finance record
CAPEX and OPEX by node and project, node and project payback, IRR, sensitivity range, and for every assumption its Variable / Value / Source URL / formula-use link (SVC-072, TBD-051). An assumption without a source is shown as such, not omitted.

Scope restrictions recorded by HOLD and REVISE are enforceable conditions, not advice: they are applied to the operating configuration (which segment, site, mechanisms and capacity are exposed) and released only by a later recorded outcome.

7.D.9 Failure handling and recovery

HOLD conditionWhat it indicatesTypical closure evidence
Safety / privacy / legal riskAn unresolved risk that the gate cannot acceptResolution or an accepted scope restriction, recorded with its owner
Unknown executionOutcomes of commands or reservations cannot be confirmedReconciled outcomes; fault-path evidence from P24
Missing evidenceA required evidence item is absentThe item, as a record
Unstaffed supportSupport or recovery coverage is not in placeStaffed queue and recovery coverage confirmed by Operations
Partner unreadinessA provider, site or energy partner cannot meet its obligationsPartner acceptance; confirmed capacity
Unreliable dataTrace quality is insufficient to compute the KPIsReconciled request and outcome records (SVC-022)
Unreconciled costCosts cannot be assigned to one owner or are counted twiceReconciled ledger; every cost to one owner (SVC-028)

A HOLD that reaches its next review trigger without closure is not silently extended; the review records either a new review trigger with reasons, a return to an earlier gate, or a stop.

7.D.10 Security, privacy and audit

The gate records are the audit trail of exposure: for any user segment / site it must be possible to show which outcome authorised the current scope, on which evidence, under which restrictions, and who owned it. Consent boundaries recorded at G1 and consent ownership agreed at G2 bound every later evaluation; a gate cannot approve use of a signal outside its recorded purpose (SVC-001). Privacy and legal risk are explicit HOLD conditions rather than items in a general risk list, so they cannot be traded against service or financial gains.

7.D.11 Measures and decision basis

The gates use the measures of P05 and add no new ones. What changes from gate to gate is the kind of evidence accepted: G1 accepts observation and baselines; G2 accepts definitions and designed comparisons; G3 accepts test traces and rehearsals; G4 accepts observed outcomes with matched inputs; G5 accepts repetition at a second site. A gate never accepts evidence of an earlier kind in place of the kind it requires — simulated acceptance does not satisfy G4 (SVC-061).

The decision basis is lexicographic: service feasibility and customer choice are checked first and are binding; net value is then judged among options that respect them. A mechanism that raises contribution by breaking an accepted passenger limit or by removing a user's option to decline is not eligible for GO.

7.D.12 Verification approach

  • Record completeness — each GO / HOLD record is checked for every required field before scope changes; a missing field blocks the change.
  • Traceability — each evidence item referenced by a record resolves to a stored decision packet, test trace or ledger extract.
  • Return-rule check — when a failed condition is recorded, the review confirms that every dependent later GO was marked as no longer current.
  • Rollback rehearsal — the rollback path named in a GO record is the one rehearsed at G3 (SVC-068).

7.D.13 Design rationale and alternatives considered

Evidence gates rather than phase gates. Calendar phases are simpler to plan but reward passing on time over passing on evidence; with shared vehicles, consent and partner capacity, an early pass can create obligations that are costly to unwind. Evidence gates accept schedule uncertainty in exchange for bounded exposure.

Three outcomes rather than two. A binary GO / NO-GO forces either premature expansion or abandonment of a mechanism with a fixable gap. REVISE allows progress under a temporary restriction with a named owner and deadline, while HOLD keeps the stronger meaning of an unresolved problem.

Return to the earliest invalidated gate. Returning only one step would leave later approvals standing on a broken assumption. Tracing back to the earliest affected gate costs rework but keeps every current GO consistent with current evidence.

Second-site repetition before expansion. First-site results combine the mechanism with local demand, provider capacity and costs. Repetition separates what transfers from what is local, which is the basis of a verified operating envelope.

7.D.14 Open points

  • G1 selection of users, zones and time windows (TBD-049).
  • Consent, capacity and custody ownership; passenger and freight gates; cost boundaries — G2 (TBD-050).
  • Finance record content and values (TBD-051); KPI targets (TBD-031).
  • MVP entry selection and boundaries (TBD-048); implementation, performance and safety validation as G3 evidence (TBD-052).

8.DDetailed specification

This section specifies the container architecture as a set of responsibilities, ownership rules and runtime behaviours: what each container may and may not do, how a channel request becomes a committed domain change and a distributed event, how the runtime zones isolate failures, and how the platform restores, reconciles and re-enables dispatch after a regional failure. It elaborates the request and event path (D08.1), the recovery state machine (D08.2) and the container placement (D08.3); the per-container functional views are in Appendix B (C01–C09).

8.D.1 Purpose and scope

The architecture is a proposed common platform on which reservation, dispatch and energy operations share one set of identities, ownership rules and events. Its central design objective is that every customer-visible commitment can be traced to exactly one owning store and one committed change, and that no failure — of a connector, a vehicle link, the broker or the regional core — can produce a duplicated effect or a commitment that the owning store does not know about.

In scope: the logical containers C01–C09 and their stores D1–D7, the trust boundary, the request path, committed-event distribution, the two runtime zones, degraded operation and regional recovery. Out of scope here and specified elsewhere: C03 internals (P09), entity keys and payloads (P10), the booking saga (P11), energy coordination (P12), remote operation (P13 onward) and roadside ingestion (P15). Hosting zones, failover mechanism, protocols, recovery objectives, latency and freshness budgets are not decided in this document; they are G2 decisions (PLT-025). The design is desk-reviewed; implementation and validation remain pending (ASM-003).

8.D.2 Actors and responsibilities

ContainerIs responsible forMust not
C01Terminating channel and console requests; identity, object / tenant access, consent, schema and source cursor checks; translating requests into authenticated domain commands; holding PlanReference (PLT-009)Decide booking outcomes or hold domain state other than PlanReference
C02Customer and provider outcomes; booking intent, terms, saga and cancellation; the D1 dispatch permitAllocate capacity directly; that is C03's D2 transaction
C03Feasibility and allocation of seats, cargo, bay, charge and work slots as one D2 transaction per bundle resource setAssume atomicity with any other store or external system (PLT-013)
C04Mission commands to the vehicle edge; the D3 command and status journal; ETA, availability and observed evidenceRelease a mission without the current D1 permit; reuse capacity whose execution is unknown (BKG-048, BKG-049)
C05Energy plans, ACKs and market commitments; capacity, setpoints and derating towards EMSTake over plant protection, which remains local (PLT-005)
C06 + C08Vehicle cases and owner leases; service cases and AI tool traces; case-type permissions on I07Allow any AI tool call to bypass command guards (PLT-006)
C07Actuals, contract and bill revisions; passenger fares, freight and shared costs; payment and payroll jobsOverwrite actuals destructively; run a payment twice (PLT-007)
C09Delivering committed events from each owner's outbox to scoped subscribers, at least onceOwn domain state; it holds no D1–D7 store

Human actors reach the platform only through C01: residents and partner channels over I01, operators and providers through scoped consoles over I02 and I06. Vehicles, EMS and meters are reached only through adapters (C04, C05, the I08 adapters), never by domain components directly.

8.D.3 Preconditions and inputs

  • A request carries an identity that C01 can authenticate and a tenant scope to which the identity has access for the object addressed.
  • Where the request uses personal signals, a consent with purpose and expiry exists and covers the use (SVC-001).
  • The request conforms to the schema version that C01 accepts for the interface; examples in P10 3.2 are conceptual payloads and the complete schemas remain open (TBD-040).
  • For calendar and partner sources, the source cursor is known so that C01 can detect replays and gaps in the source stream.
  • Domain components run with fenced writer ownership: only the current writer instance of an owned store can commit (PLT-012).

8.D.4 Behaviour

Main flow — channel request to committed event (D08.1):

  1. A channel or console sends a request over HTTPS / I01, I02 or I06.
  2. C01 applies identity, object / tenant access, consent, schema and source cursor checks; any failure returns a rejection to the caller and nothing crosses the trust boundary (PLT-001).
  3. C01 forwards an authenticated domain command to the owning component (PLT-002).
  4. C02 persists the booking change together with its outbox entry in one local commit on D1 (PLT-011).
  5. Where capacity is needed, C02 calls C03 over I03; C03 performs one D2 transaction for the bundle resource set and commits its outbox entry atomically with it.
  6. C03 returns a guarded outcome; C02 finalises D1 by compare-and-set on the booking revision.
  7. When a mission is due, C04 obtains the current D1 permit, issues the mission over I04 and journals command and status in D3.
  8. Each owner's outbox relay hands the committed change to C09, which delivers BookingChanged, AllocationCommitted, MissionObserved and the other committed events to scoped subscribers (PLT-014, PLT-021).
  9. Each subscriber processes the envelope through its idempotent inbox and revision check (PLT-015, PLT-016).

Alternative flow — equipment feedback. Equipment state from home, corporate or district EMS returns over I05 through the C05 adapters (the dashed route in 1.1). C05 updates D4 and publishes EnergyUpdated; C03 consumes the change as a versioned energy capability input, never as a shared revision with the resource snapshot (BKG-008).

Alternative flow — operator action. An operator acting on a case enters through C01 with a console identity; C06 + C08 apply the permissions of the case type on I07 and any resulting request to a vehicle passes the command guards of C04. An AI-drafted action follows the same path and the same guards.

Exception flows.

  1. Connector failure. When a provider or channel connector fails, C01 may continue to accept local intake. Confirmation is withheld until every mandatory dependency for that booking is available; the user sees an accepted request, not a confirmed booking (PLT-023).
  2. Stale vehicle / site state. When the evidence for a vehicle or site is older than its freshness budget (TBD-006), C03 blocks the affected capacity from new allocation (PLT-024).
  3. Unknown execution. When C04 cannot confirm whether a mission command took effect, the capacity it touches is not reused; C04 queries by the original command ID rather than resending with a new one (BKG-049, PLT-029).
  4. Broker unavailable. Owners keep committing; entries accumulate in their outboxes and are relayed when C09 recovers. No committed change is lost, and no subscriber sees a change that was not committed.
  5. Unappliable event. A subscriber that cannot apply an event after fetching the gap quarantines it; C09 raises a poison-event alert (PLT-018).

8.D.5 Rules and invariants

  1. R8.1 Only authenticated domain commands cross the trust boundary inward, and only scoped event subscriptions cross it outward (PLT-002, PLT-003).
  2. R8.2 Each store has exactly one writing component; other components read by reference or through events (PLT-009, PLT-010).
  3. R8.3 A store change and its outbox entry are committed together or not at all (PLT-011).
  4. R8.4 Atomic guarantees cover D2 only; cross-store and external effects are coordinated by saga with reconciliation (PLT-013, ASM-007).
  5. R8.5 Dispatch requires the current D1 permit; unknown execution blocks reuse (BKG-047, BKG-048, BKG-049).
  6. R8.6 Delivery is at least once; correctness comes from idempotent inboxes and per-aggregate revision checks, not from the broker (PLT-014–PLT-016).
  7. R8.7 Replay builds separate projections and runs idempotent effect handlers; replay produces no external effect (PLT-017).
  8. R8.8 Plant protection is local and does not depend on the regional core (PLT-005, ASM-016).
  9. R8.9 No AI tool call bypasses command guards; AI may draft or summarise within task scope but cannot independently authorise ADS movement (PLT-006, ASM-015).
  10. R8.10 Optional equipment, JV or eVTOL capabilities attach only through capability interfaces and do not change the ownership rules of the primary service (PLT-008).

8.D.6 Data and state

D1C02Booking revision, terms, intent, saga state, dispatch permit, cancellationBookingChanged events; permit query by C04
D2C03Route / segment capacity, bundles and intervalsAllocationCommitted events; I03 results
D3C04Command and status journal: what was sent, received, accepted and observedMissionObserved events
D4C05Energy plans, ACKs and market commitmentsEnergyUpdated events; capability reads by C03

The durable state of the regional core holds D1–D7 as logical stores, with each owner's outbox and the command journal alongside its domain data so that they share one backup and one restore point. Resource constraints are enforced inside D2, not in application code alone, so that a concurrent request cannot pass a check that the store would reject. Projections used by consoles and other containers are derived data: they can be discarded and rebuilt from committed events at any time, and are never a source for a decision that commits capacity.

8.D.7 Interfaces used

InterfaceBetweenRole in this chapter

I03C02 → C03Quote / hold / atomic replacement

Protocols for I03, I04, I05, I07, I08 and the C09 backbone are G2 decisions (TBD-003).

8.D.8 Deployment and isolation

The runtime is split into a regional core and an operations zone (D08.3). The regional core is the active reservation authority: it runs the request workers of C01, C02, C03 and C05 and holds the durable state. The operations zone holds integration and projections: the C09 broker and consumers, and the external adapters for C04, I05, I06 and I08.

  • Stateless request workers. Workers in the core keep no domain state between requests; they can be added, removed or restarted without coordination. Tenant / object access guards run in every worker, not only at the edge, so a routing error cannot cross tenants (PLT-004).
  • Fenced writer ownership. At most one writer instance holds the right to commit to an owned store. A stale writer that resumes after a partition cannot commit, because its fence is no longer current (PLT-012).
  • Adapters isolate external behaviour. Each adapter keeps a protocol + retry journal, reconciles with its provider and offers local edge fallback (PLT-022). A slow or failing provider consumes adapter capacity, not core capacity.
  • Projections isolate reads. Console and reporting load is served from projections in the operations zone, so heavy reads do not contend with D2 transactions.

Placement of these zones into hosting zones, and the failover mechanism between them, are G2 decisions (TBD-001, TBD-002).

8.D.9 Failure handling and recovery

Regional recovery follows RESTORE → RECONCILE → ENABLE DISPATCH (D08.2). Local intake may remain available throughout; confirmation and dispatch wait for the guards.

  1. RESTORE. Domain state, consent, outboxes and command history are restored from a recovery-consistent backup, so that every outbox entry corresponds to a committed change in the same restore point (PLT-026).
  2. RECONCILE. Projections are rebuilt from committed events without effect. Every external effect that may have occurred after the restore point — mission commands, energy reservations, provider holds, payments — is verified with its counterparty by its original ID (PLT-027). An effect that cannot be confirmed quarantines the affected resource; the original intent or command ID is queried; if the query budget expires, the uncertainty is retained as an owned exception (PLT-029, TBD-027).
  3. ENABLE DISPATCH. The writer is fenced, vehicle and site freshness is confirmed, and an operator approves readiness (PLT-028). Capacity whose state is still stale stays blocked.
FailureContainmentRecovery
Connector downLocal intake continues; confirmation withheldAdapter retry journal; provider reconciliation by original ID
Vehicle link lostVehicle-local fallback; capacity blocked as unknownQuery by command ID; reconcile D3 journal (P13)
Broker downOutboxes retain committed entriesRelay resumes; inbox deduplication absorbs repeats
Consumer behindLag alert; projections marked staleCatch up from C09; fetch gaps per aggregate
Poison eventEvent quarantined; alert raisedOwned investigation; reapply after correction
Writer partitionFence prevents stale commitNew writer takes fence; reconcile prior accepted effects (P24 T-R06)
Regional core lostDispatch disabled; plant protection and vehicle fallback stay localRESTORE → RECONCILE → ENABLE DISPATCH

Recovery objectives for the core and for D1–D7 are G2 decisions (TBD-004).

8.D.10 Security, privacy and audit

The trust boundary is enforced in depth: C01 authenticates and authorises every request, workers re-check tenant / object access, and every key and foreign key carries the tenant scope so that a reference cannot resolve outside it (PLT-030). Consent is checked at entry and restored with domain state, so that consent and the domain state it governs are recovered to the same restore point. Event subscriptions are scoped, and every envelope carries its tenant, so consumers receive only what their scope allows.

Auditability comes from the stores themselves: D1 records intent and terms per revision, D3 records every command and status, D5 / D7 record cases and AI tool traces, D6 never overwrites actuals. Operator and AI actions are therefore reconstructable from the owning stores without relying on logs outside them.

8.D.11 Observability and operations

  • Event flow — C09 raises lag and poison-event alerts (PLT-018); projections expose how far they are behind their sources so that consoles can show staleness.
  • Adapters — retry journals and reconciliation results are observable per provider, so a provider that silently drops requests is visible as unreconciled entries.
  • Uncertainty — blocked capacity due to unknown execution or stale evidence is visible as such, with its owner, so operations can distinguish "no capacity" from "capacity of unknown state".
  • Readiness — ENABLE DISPATCH is an operator-approved step; the approval and the checks behind it are recorded.

8.D.12 Verification approach

  • Boundary tests — requests failing each C01 check are rejected and leave no domain change (PLT-001).
  • Atomicity tests — a crash between store change and outbox write leaves neither, or both (PLT-011).
  • Duplicate and reorder tests — duplicated and reordered envelopes produce one effect and a gap fetch (P24 T-R01, T-R04).
  • Fencing tests — a partitioned writer that resumes cannot commit; prior accepted effects are reconciled (T-R06).
  • Recovery drill — restore from backup, rebuild projections, verify external effects by original IDs and confirm that dispatch stays disabled until readiness is approved (P24 17.2).
  • Degraded-mode tests — with a connector down, intake is accepted and confirmation withheld; with stale site state, the capacity is blocked.

8.D.13 Design rationale and alternatives considered

Single writer per store rather than a shared database. A shared schema written by several components would make ownership of each outcome ambiguous and couple their release cycles. One writer per store makes every invariant enforceable in one place and makes recovery a per-store question.

Transactional outbox rather than dual writes. Writing to a store and publishing to a broker separately can lose or invent events on failure. Committing the outbox with the change ensures that every published event corresponds to a committed change and that no committed change is left unpublished.

At-least-once with idempotent consumers rather than exactly-once delivery. Exactly-once across a broker and many consumers is hard to guarantee end to end, especially through external adapters. At-least-once delivery with deduplication and revision checks puts the guarantee where the effect is applied.

Local atomicity and reconciled sagas rather than distributed commit. EMS, providers and vehicles are external systems that cannot join a distributed transaction. Restricting atomicity to D2 and handling the rest with explicit unknown outcomes and reconciliation is honest about what can be guaranteed (ASM-007).

Gated re-enable of dispatch. Automatic resumption after restore could dispatch against capacity whose external state changed during the outage. Requiring reconciliation, fencing, freshness and operator approval trades recovery time for the guarantee that no vehicle moves on unverified state.

8.D.14 Open points

  • Hosting zones (TBD-001); failover mechanism (TBD-002); protocols (TBD-003); recovery objectives (TBD-004); latency budgets (TBD-005); freshness budgets (TBD-006) — all decided at G2.
  • Complete API schemas (TBD-040); equipment / JV / eVTOL options (TBD-038).
  • Implementation, performance and safety validation as G3 evidence (TBD-052).

2.3Selected reservation transitions and replacement constraints

Replacement holds new capacity before retiring old. Swap applies only to unstarted allocations. Started/unknown missions retain occupancy until physical clearance. PENDING does not expire on quote TTL. Cancellation uses P11; shared seats enforce summed capacity per segment.

Shared rides and cargo require segment capacity, route revision and distinct booking outcomes (P29–P30). Count the vehicle cycle once, including empty travel, boarding, cargo dwell, turnaround and energy. Reserve loading bays, staff and hub capacity separately (P25–P26).
