23.DDetailed specification

This section specifies the activity saga that couples a provider service (care outing, after-school care, community event) with a mobility reservation, and the constrained pipeline through which AI assistance may contribute to it. It defines the step order and the decision points of the swimlane in 16.1, the compensation and reconciliation behaviour when one side commits and the other does not, the service guards per activity type, the calendar and commercial-API boundaries, and the authority limits, release stages and review of AI assistance in 16.2. C02 is the coordinator throughout; it never assumes a distributed atomic commit across provider and transport.

23.D.1 Purpose and scope

Some trips in the target service exist only because of an activity: a care-home outing, a pick-up from after-school care, a trip to a community event. The value to the resident lies in both parts happening together; the operational risk lies in one part succeeding while the other fails. The saga coordinates the two as separate reservations, each owned by its own system and provider, and makes every partial outcome visible, owned and recoverable.

In scope: intent normalisation, parallel holds, offer and acceptance, commit through the D1 saga and outbox, verification of all required commits, compensation and reconciliation, re-entry on ETA change, service guards, calendar-originated intent, and the AI tool pipeline. Out of scope: the C03 feasibility and allocation rules (P09, P25), the joint reservation transaction itself (P11 4.1), and the provider's internal staffing and care processes, which remain the provider's responsibility (BKG-060).

23.D.2 Actors and responsibilities

Actor / containerResponsible forNot responsible for
Resident / staff (or guardian)Stating need and consent: time, place, support; accepting terms that include activity and travel costCoordinating provider and transport
Activity providerHolding and confirming the activity slot, staff and terms; service delivery, staffing and handover obligationsVehicle allocation
C02 Coordinator (D1)Normalising intent, placing parallel holds, making the offer, committing intent with the saga and outbox, verifying commits, compensating and reconciling, owning exceptions and customer outcomesDeciding vehicle feasibility
C03 Mobility (D2)Holding and committing the mobility bundle: vehicle, bay, chargeProvider-side confirmation
C01 API gateway + adaptersChannel intake, consent and source cursor; provider console accessBooking decisions
AI assistance (C06 + C08, D7)Extracting and normalising fields, drafting proposals within task scopeAuthorising commands outside its stage and allowlist; authorising motion in any stage
Staff reviewerDeciding proposals that are out of scope, low confidence, add cost or involve a custody exception; reviewing observed outcomes—

23.D.3 Preconditions and inputs

  1. The requester is identified and has consent for the stated purpose, with expiry and withdrawal explicit (I01). For school care, guardian authority is part of the service guard and is checked from the first hold onward (23.D.5).
  2. The need is stated with time, place and required support, either directly or from a calendar source through a PlanReference (sourceEventId, sourceRevision, consentId, purpose, expiresAt).
  3. The provider is reachable through a commercial API that offers access and hold / commit / cancel support, or through an owned manual workflow (BKG-065, TBD-039).
  4. C03 can quote and hold for the requested windows; conditions are captured under a conditionsRev so that later changes are detectable.

23.D.4 Behaviour: activity saga

The swimlane is drawn in 16.1; the uncertain-commit branch as messages in D23.1; the fields read and written by each step in D23.2.

Main flow

  1. Need / consent. The resident or staff states the need; C01 passes the confirmed fields to C02.
  2. Normalise intent. C02 creates one intent with its source and conditionsRev (BKG-053). The intent identity is stable across later revisions.
  3. Parallel holds. C02 requests the activity hold from the provider over I06 (slot, staff, terms, expiry) and the mobility hold from C03 over I03 (vehicle, bay, charge) at the same time (BKG-054). Parallel placement shortens the time during which one hold is waiting for the other to be known.
  4. All holds valid? If both holds are valid and unexpired, C02 makes one offer covering activity and travel cost. If either is invalid or unknown, C02 raises an owned exception and releases the holds that are known (BKG-055).
  5. Accept terms. The resident or staff accepts; the acceptance carries acceptedTermsRev. An acceptance against changed or expired terms is rejected and terms are refreshed.
  6. Commit intent. C02 persists the commit intent in the D1 saga together with its outbox entry before contacting either side (BKG-056). This makes the commit recoverable after a C02 restart.
  7. Confirm activity and commit bundle. C02 asks the provider to confirm (providerRef + state) and C03 to commit the bundle (bundleId + revision).
  8. All required commits verified? Only when both confirmations are verified does C02 permit the service (BKG-057). Verified commitments then lead to a permitted service and, after execution, to actuals.

Alternative flows

  • Offer not accepted before hold expiry. Both holds lapse under their own expiry; C02 records the outcome and makes no commit.
  • ETA change. A change in expected arrival re-enters the saga with a new revision (BKG-062): the provider and C03 are asked to revise against the new times, the old commitments stay until the replacement is final, and the request identity is preserved.
  • Cancellation by the requester. C02 records the cancellation against the intent and cancels each side; cancellation after the dispatch permit is handled as cancel / replan of the in-flight mission (BKG-052).
  • Manual provider. Where the provider has no hold / commit / cancel API, each saga step that touches the provider becomes an owned manual task with owner and dueAt in the WorkOrder; the saga logic is unchanged.

Exception flows

  1. Commit outcome unknown. The reservation moves to RECONCILING and C02 queries the original intent on the uncertain side before doing anything else; capacity stays blocked while the effect is unknown (BKG-026).
  2. One side confirmed, the other rejected. C02 compensates the confirmed side (for example, cancels the confirmed activity), records the persisted result and any fees, and gives the resident a customer outcome with alternatives (BKG-058).
  3. Compensation fails or is uncertain. The failure stays owned and reconciled (BKG-045); it is escalated with a deadline rather than retried indefinitely.
  4. Service guard fails after commit (for example, care-staff capacity withdrawn). The service is not permitted; C02 treats it as a partial failure and follows the compensation path.

23.D.5 Service guards per activity type

The guard is evaluated at hold, at commit verification and again before the service is permitted, because each of its terms can change in between (BKG-061).

Activity typeGuard termsTypical failure handled
Care outingRequired assistance + care-staff capacityAssistance cannot be provided at the stop; staff no longer available
After-school careGuardian authority + verified handoverHandover counterpart not verified; guardian authority not current — a custody exception that goes to a human decision
Community eventVenue / stop + host capacityStop not usable; host capacity reached

23.D.6 Rules and invariants

R23.1
Provider and transport reservations are never treated as one distributed transaction (BKG-059, BKG-019).
R23.2
An offer is made only when every required hold is valid; an invalid or unknown hold yields an owned exception that releases only the known holds (BKG-055).
R23.3
The commit intent and its outbox are persisted in D1 before any external commit is requested (BKG-056).
R23.4
Service is permitted only after all required commits are verified (BKG-057).
R23.5
C02 queries before it compensates; it never compensates on an assumed failure (BKG-058).
R23.6
Failed compensation stays owned and reconciled; fees and failed recovery are tracked.
R23.7
An ETA change re-enters the saga with a new revision and keeps the request identity (BKG-062).
R23.8
Calendar changes produce proposed intent and never auto-book by default; sync deletion or resync never erases D1 bookings (BKG-063, BKG-064).
R23.9
AI output becomes an effect only as an idempotent domain command under role, tool allowlist and lease, behind independent guards for consent and accepted terms (OPS-090).
R23.10
Service AI cannot authorise motion in any release stage (OPS-089).

23.D.7 Data and state

Provider-side state lives in ActivitySaga / WorkOrder in D1 (tenantId, sagaId / workOrderId, bookingId, bundleId, providerRef, slotRef, staffRefs[], conditionsRev, acceptedTermsRev, state, owner, dueAt, evidenceRef). Mobility-side state lives in ResourceBundle and its ResourceInterval entries in D2. The Booking in D1 links the two through bookingId and currentBundleId and is finalised by CAS on expectedBookingRev.

  • Revisions. conditionsRev captures what was asked; acceptedTermsRev what was accepted; bundleRev what was allocated. A mismatch between them is a reason to refresh, never to proceed.
  • Ownership. Every WorkOrder that represents an open obligation — a manual provider step, a compensation, cleaning, inspection or handover task — carries owner and dueAt, so that an open saga always has a responsible person.
  • Evidence. evidenceRef on the WorkOrder records the provider confirmation or handover evidence used to verify the commit; a confirmation without evidence does not satisfy R23.4.
  • Events. Saga changes are published through the outbox as events on C09, so downstream consumers observe one ordered history per aggregate.

23.D.8 Behaviour: AI assistance pipeline

The pipeline of 16.2 is drawn as messages in D23.3. Its principle is that the AI's output is a proposal; authority comes from deterministic checks and from the human or policy that is entitled to decide.

  1. Observe / extract. From conversation and event evidence, the AI extracts the fields of a need (time, place, support, party) and marks missing fields explicitly instead of guessing them.
  2. Validate / propose. The proposal is validated against the typed schema of the target domain command and against consent; deterministic constraints (for example hold expiry, accepted terms, service guards) are evaluated by the domain service, not by the model.
  3. Route. A proposal that is outside scope, low confidence, adds cost or involves a custody exception goes to a human decision (OPS-091).
  4. Authorise / execute. Role, tool allowlist and lease decide whether the proposal may be executed automatically; execution is always an idempotent domain command, so a repeated AI call cannot create a second effect (OPS-090).
  5. Verify / review. The observed outcome is compared with the proposal and reviewed; findings feed offline improvement, and any change to the model reaches production only through offline evaluation and a versioned release (OPS-092).

Release stages move from shadow comparison (the AI proposes, staff decide, proposals are compared), to staff-approved actions (each command requires approval), to bounded automatic tasks (commands within allowlist and lease, with exceptions to humans). Progression between stages is a release decision with its own evidence (TBD-044); a stage can be reverted without changing the domain services, because the guards are independent of the AI.

23.D.9 Calendar and commercial integration

A calendar event is a statement of plan, not of commitment. A new or changed event produces a proposed intent for confirmation; it does not book by default (BKG-063). Deletion of an event, or a full resync of the calendar connector, cannot erase a D1 booking (BKG-064): the booking has its own lifecycle and is cancelled through I02, not by the calendar connector. Commercial provider APIs are used for reservations only where they provide access and hold / commit / cancel; otherwise the provider step is an owned manual workflow (BKG-065), because a reservation that cannot be held or cancelled cannot take part in compensation.

23.D.10 Interfaces used

  • I01 channel intake: need, consent and confirmed fields; PlanReference for calendar sources.
  • I06 activity hold and confirmation: hold, confirm, compensate / reconcile with the provider.
  • I03 joint reservation: mobility hold and CommitBundle to C03 (Appendix B C03).
  • I02 booking commit / amend / cancel and customer outcome.
  • I07 for AI tool calls in the operations domain; I07 permissions differ by case type and no AI path bypasses command guards.

23.D.11 Failure handling and recovery

FailureResponseRecovery condition
Provider does not answer a holdHold treated as unknown; owned exception; mobility hold released if knownProvider answer or expiry of the request
Mobility commit uncertain, activity confirmedQuery the original intent; capacity stays blocked; no compensation yetBundle committed (proceed) or rejected (compensate activity)
Activity confirmation lostQuery the provider by providerRef; mobility stays committed but service not permittedVerified confirmation or explicit reject
Compensation incurs fees or failsFees and failed recovery tracked; exception owned with dueAtRecorded outcome accepted by the owner
C02 restarts mid-sagaRecovery from the D1 saga and outbox; outstanding external calls repeated idempotentlySaga state consistent with both sides' answers
Calendar connector resyncsProposed intents regenerated; existing bookings untouchedProposals reconciled against bookings
AI proposal invalid or out of scopeRejected by schema or routed to human decision; trace kept in D7Human decision recorded

23.D.12 Security, privacy and audit

Consent is purpose-bound and carries expiry; holds and commits are rejected when consent is missing or expired, and the independent guards enforce consent and accepted terms regardless of whether the request came from a person or the AI. Guardian authority for school care and custody handover evidence are the most sensitive data in this flow; they are visible only to the roles that need them for the task, and a custody exception is always decided by a person (OPS-091). Every AI call leaves a tool trace in D7 linked to the service case, so a reviewer can see what was extracted, what was proposed, which guard decided and what happened. Keys and foreign keys include tenant scope (ASM-009).

23.D.13 Observability and operations

Per saga, the following are recorded so that partial failures are visible rather than averaged away: holds placed and their outcome per side, offers made and accepted, commits requested and verified per side, compensations started, completed and failed, fees incurred, re-entries on ETA change, and owned exceptions with their age. For the AI pipeline: proposals by outcome (executed, approved, rejected, routed to human), routing reason, and differences between proposal and observed outcome in shadow comparison, which is the evidence for stage progression.

23.D.14 Verification approach

  • Partial-commit matrix. For each combination of provider and mobility outcome (confirmed, rejected, unknown), verify the next step: proceed, compensate, or query; no combination may permit service without both verified commits (D23.1).
  • Restart. Stop C02 after the D1 commit intent and before each external call; recovery must not duplicate a provider or bundle effect.
  • Service guards. Withdraw care-staff capacity, guardian authority or host capacity at each guard point and verify that service is not permitted.
  • ETA re-entry. Shift times and verify that request identity is preserved and old commitments remain until the replacement is final.
  • Calendar. Delete and resync calendar sources and verify that D1 bookings remain.
  • AI authority. Attempt AI-originated commands outside the allowlist, without lease, with missing consent and for motion; each must be denied and traced (T-R08, P24 17.1).

23.D.15 Design rationale and alternatives considered

Saga instead of distributed transaction. Provider systems and commercial APIs do not participate in a shared atomic commit, and many providers are manual. A saga with explicit holds, verified commits and compensation works with any partner that can hold and cancel, and degrades to an owned manual workflow for those that cannot. The cost is that partial states exist and must be owned; the design makes them visible instead of pretending they cannot happen.

Parallel rather than sequential holds. Holding the activity first and the vehicle second lengthens the time the first hold is idle and increases the chance that it expires. Parallel holds with a single decision point reduce that window; releasing only known holds keeps the exception path safe.

Query before compensation. Compensating on a timeout can cancel a commitment that in fact succeeded, which can create a worse customer outcome than waiting. Querying first turns a timeout into a known outcome wherever the counterparty can answer.

AI as proposer, guards as deciders. Letting the model decide directly would make consent, terms and custody depend on model behaviour. Keeping deterministic guards independent allows the AI to be improved, staged or withdrawn without changing what the system permits.

23.D.16 Open points

  • Commercial API support per provider, otherwise owned manual workflow (TBD-039).
  • AI release stage progression and the evidence for each stage (TBD-044).
  • Consent, capacity and custody ownership and cost boundaries — G2 (TBD-050).
  • Complete API schemas for I03 and I07 (TBD-040); protocol choices at G2 (TBD-003).

24.DDetailed specification

This section specifies how the remote-operation design is verified and how verification evidence governs release (RM-11). It defines what a fault-injection run must record and how its oracle decides, details each planned case T-R01 to T-R08 as precondition, injection and observable invariant, specifies the shared recovery behaviour of 17.2 that every container must exhibit after a fault with an uncertain effect, lists the acceptance extensions owed by other chapters, and sets out the gate process G1–G5 with its parallel workstreams, decision records and return path. All cases are planned tests; none is reported as passed.

24.D.1 Purpose and scope

A design whose safety and service claims rest on invariants — no duplicate effect, no motion on stale evidence, no unowned case — is only as credible as the evidence that those invariants hold under faults. The purpose of this chapter is to make that evidence reproducible and to tie release decisions to it rather than to schedule. Remote-operation requirements join the PaaS acceptance plan so that one release decision covers booking, allocation, energy, remote operation and recovery together (OPS-093).

In scope: fault-injection cases and their oracles, the orthogonal-state cross-products, the shared PaaS recovery invariant, the referenced roadside, capacity and settlement acceptance, and the gate process with its evidence chain. Out of scope: test tooling choices, concrete pass thresholds (set by the parameter owners of P22 15.3), and the safety case of the ADS itself, which the vehicle owner provides.

24.D.2 Actors and responsibilities

Actor / workstreamResponsible for
Platform / QA / operationsContracts, fault tests, trained fallback, security, recovery and human trials; maintaining the fault-injection cases and their oracles; producing G3 evidence
Product / local serviceDemand, service quality and economics; responsibilities and operating plan; the observed outcomes used at G4
Partners / energyEMS capability and access agreements; connector recovery and repeatability
Gate decision ownersOwner, residual risk / restriction and signed decision at each gate; ownership by gate follows P07 (for example, Engineering + Operations at G3)
ADS ownerVehicle-side behaviour under injected faults; evidence for onboard accept / reject, fence and journal

24.D.3 Run record and oracle

Every fault-injection run produces one record (OPS-094); a run without a complete record does not count as evidence.

Scenario / ODD slice
The operating conditions under which the run is valid. A result never generalises beyond its slice.
Initial state
Vehicle, case, booking, bundle and energy state at the start, so that the run can be repeated.
Revisions
Software, schema, policy, map, calibration and parameter revisions in effect; a change in any revision invalidates reuse of the result.
Injected fault
What was injected, where and when, recorded independently of what the system observed.
Trace
The events of all affected containers, with observedAt, receivedAt and sequence, sufficient to replay the decision path.
Oracle result
Pass or fail for each invariant, with the evidence the oracle used.
Level
SIL, HIL, operator or vehicle trial as applicable; the level is part of the evidence, because an operator trial demonstrates what a simulation cannot, and the reverse.

The oracle reads recorded fields, not the system's own verdict. For example, "no duplicate effect" is decided from the vehicle-side journal and the observed execution, not from the centre's belief that it sent once. The fields each oracle reads are listed in D24.1.

24.D.5 Orthogonal-state cross-products

Testing one state chain at a time misses defects where two dimensions disagree. The following combinations are tested explicitly (OPS-095, P18 11.3):

  • DDT_ACTIVE + RA_PENDING. The ADS continues approved local behaviour while assistance is pending; no assistance outcome implies a mode transition.
  • MRC + stale evidence. An achieved MRC reported on stale evidence does not make the vehicle ready to drive or eligible for release.
  • CLOSED case + critical fault. A new critical fault after closure reopens a case and keeps the vehicle held; closure does not mask it.
  • Fresh telemetry + unresolved command. Current telemetry does not resolve a command whose terminal evidence is missing; capacity stays blocked.

24.D.6 Shared PaaS recovery behaviour

The recovery invariant of 17.2 applies to every container that can cause an external effect: C02 sagas, C03 allocations, C04 commands, C05 energy plans and C06 cases. Its state view is drawn in D24.2.

  1. Quarantine. On a fault where the effect is uncertain, the affected resource is held: no reuse, no new commitment against it (OPS-096).
  2. Preserve times. Observed and source times are kept as received, so that later evidence can be ordered against them (OPS-096).
  3. Query. The original intent or cmdId is queried; no new ID is generated to "try again" (OPS-004). The query loop runs while its budget remains (TBD-027).
  4. Known outcome. If the outcome becomes known, state is recovered from the durable journal and projections are rebuilt without re-executing effects.
  5. Owned exception. If the deadline is reached with the outcome still unknown, the uncertainty is retained, not resolved by assumption; an owned exception is opened with deadline, backup owner and fallback (OPS-097).
  6. Late evidence. Terminal evidence arriving after the exception was opened moves the item to a known outcome; the exception owner closes it with that evidence.
  7. Re-entry. The resource returns to use only through authorised re-entry on current evidence and valid state, which for vehicles means the release predicate (P18 11.3).

24.D.8 Gate process

Gates are evidence checkpoints, not calendar phases (D24.3, P07). The three workstreams of 17.3 run in parallel and contribute to every gate.

  1. G1 Target. Users, zones and time windows are selected (TBD-049); service and cost baselines are traceable.
  2. G2 Requirements. The G2 decisions are recorded: hosting zones, failover mechanism, protocols, RPO / RTO, latency and freshness budgets (TBD-001–TBD-006). The further parameters of P22 15.3 each need a unit, rationale and boundary test from their owner where one is named; the document states no gate for them (TBD-007–TBD-010).
  3. G3 Pilot ready. The run records of 24.D.3 exist for T-R01 to T-R08 and the cross-products at the applicable levels; trained fallback, security and recovery trials are complete; partner connector recovery is demonstrated.
  4. G4 Continue. Observed outcomes from the pilot replace planned results: demand, service quality, economics and incident handling as actually experienced.
  5. G5 Expand. Onboarding of a further site and its partners is shown to be repeatable within a verified operating envelope.

Each gate records the owner, the residual risk or restriction and a signed decision of GO, HOLD or REVISE. A failed condition returns the work to the earliest gate whose assumption it invalidates; scope stays held until the named owner closes the evidence gap. Schedule alone never passes a gate.

24.D.9 Rules and invariants

R24.1
Planned tests are never reported as passed results; only run records with oracle results are evidence.
R24.2
A run record is incomplete, and does not count, if any of scenario / ODD slice, initial state, revisions, injected fault, trace or oracle result is missing (OPS-094).
R24.3
Oracles decide from recorded observations, independent of the system's own status reporting.
R24.4
After an uncertain effect, the affected resource is quarantined, the original intent or cmdId is queried and projections are rebuilt without effect (OPS-096).
R24.5
Uncertainty that outlives its deadline is retained as an owned exception, never resolved by assumption (OPS-097).
R24.6
Release requires reproducible evidence and operating readiness; G3 cannot pass on simulation alone where operator or vehicle trials are applicable.
R24.7
Every gate decision is signed and records owner and residual restriction; a HOLD has a named closure owner.

24.D.10 Data and evidence management

Release evidence comprises input revision, scenario / seed, execution trace, metric definitions, pass / fail by condition, residual restriction and accountable decision (CAP-064). Every run and every failure is preserved (CAP-060); a failed run that was later fixed remains in the record, because the failure is evidence of what the test can detect. Evidence is linked to the requirement IDs it exercises, so the coverage of Appendix C can be read in both directions: which tests cover a requirement, and which requirements a test covers.

24.D.11 Failure handling in verification

  • Non-reproducible result. A run that cannot be repeated from its record is treated as missing evidence, which is a HOLD reason under P07.
  • Intermittent failure. An invariant violated in any run is a failure, even if other runs pass; the case stays open until the cause is understood.
  • Oracle gap. If an invariant cannot be decided from recorded fields, the missing observation is a design defect to be fixed in the system, not a reason to accept the run.
  • Environment limitation. Where a fault cannot be injected at a given level, the record states the level used and the limitation becomes a residual restriction at the gate.

24.D.12 Security, privacy and audit

Fault-injection runs that use recorded media or passenger data follow the same purpose limitation, scoped access and retention as operational evidence (OPS-087). Audit tests cover cross-tenant access, expired authority, future timestamps, unknown clock bounds and duplicate effects (OPS-088). Gate decisions and their evidence are retained with signatures so that a later reviewer can establish what was known at the time of each decision.

24.D.13 Design rationale and alternatives considered

Observable invariants instead of scripted expected outputs. A script that expects a specific message sequence breaks whenever timing changes and can pass while the safety property fails. Invariants such as "at most one effect per commandId" or "every open branch has an owner" remain valid across implementations and are what the design actually claims.

Evidence gates instead of phase gates. A calendar plan rewards passing on time; an evidence gate rewards passing correctly. The return path to the earliest invalidated gate prevents a late discovery from being patched locally while its root assumption remains wrong.

Parallel workstreams. Running product, platform and partner evidence sequentially would delay discovery of partner or demand constraints until after the platform is built. Parallel workstreams feeding every gate surface those constraints early.

24.D.14 Open points

  • Implementation, performance and safety validation — pending, G3 evidence (TBD-052).
  • Query budget for unresolved commands (TBD-027).
  • Freshness and latency budgets used by oracles — G2 (TBD-005, TBD-006).
  • EMS capability and access agreements for the partners / energy workstream (TBD-035).
  • Roadside thresholds per use case (TBD-016).
  • MVP entry conditions (TBD-048).

25.DDetailed specification

This section specifies how C03 converts demand by zone and time into reachable supply and binding commitments, how fleet capacity is accounted for so that no vehicle is counted twice, how vehicle workload and spatial / peak feasibility are screened, and how finite hub resources are allocated as time intervals. It defines the planning-interval evaluation step by step, the meaning of each term in the reachability and conservation relations of 18.1–18.2, the interval rules per hub resource in 18.3, failure behaviour when vehicle or site evidence is stale, and how capacity alternatives are compared and reported.

25.D.1 Purpose and scope

Fleet size and hub count describe what is owned; they do not describe what can be promised. A vehicle that is ready on the wrong side of the service area, a hub whose connectors are all occupied, or a cleaning position without qualified staff contributes nothing to a pickup that is due now. The purpose of this chapter is to make capacity a computed, time- and location-specific quantity that C03 evaluates for each request and that planning evaluates for each alternative under the same demand.

In scope: the C03 evaluation at each planning interval, insertion into existing routes, fleet-state conservation, the vehicle workload screen, spatial and peak-time checks, hub resource allocation and the observable outcomes. Out of scope: the candidate generator and ranking internals (P09 2.1), replenishment timing at the hub (P26), degraded service modes (P27), measure definitions and scenario method (P28) and shared-ride constraints in detail (P29).

25.D.2 Actors and responsibilities

Actor / containerResponsible for
C02 Booking / activities (D1)Submitting requests with terms and windows; offering the hold to the customer; confirming only after verified commit (CAP-005)
C03 Joint reservation authority (D2)Reachability, insertion and constraint evaluation; holding the complete resource bundle; returning binding reasons; fleet-state accounting; hub interval allocation; reporting unmet demand (Appendix B C03)
C04 Fleet / vehicle adapterObserved vehicle position, ready time, ETA and availability, with observation quality
C05 Energy / EMS adapters and site EMSEnergy capability per site and window with capabilityRev and age; derating and outage information
Planning / operations ownerThe planning record, the availability policy, operational reserve and comparison of alternatives; agreeing intercity transfer authority

25.D.3 Preconditions and inputs

  1. A planning record exists with zone / time interval, OD input, initial vehicle positions, hub resources, availability policy and service windows (CAP-008).
  2. The request carries passenger and shipment OD and windows, party, access needs, cargo mass and volume, and its lead time relative to departure.
  3. Vehicle observations from C04, the resource snapshot from D2 and the energy capability from C05 are available as separate versioned inputs, each with its own revision and age; they are not assumed to share one revision (BKG-008).
  4. Each input is checked for freshness before use. A vehicle or site whose state is stale is not counted as supply; its capacity is blocked until current evidence returns.

25.D.4 Behaviour: evaluation at a planning interval

The message view is D25.1.

Main flow

  1. C02 submits Plan(terms, windows) with OD, party, access, cargo mass / volume.
  2. C03 reads, in parallel, vehicle position, ready time, ETA and availability from C04; resource intervals and revisions from D2; and site energy capability from C05.
  3. For each candidate vehicle v, C03 tests reachability: t_ready,v + travelTime(v, origin, departure time) ≤ latestPickup (CAP-001). Here t_ready,v is the time at which v has finished its current committed work, including any required replenishment and turnaround, at its expected position; travelTime is evaluated for the actual departure time, not as a time-independent average; latestPickup is the end of the accepted pickup window.
  4. For each reachable vehicle, C03 forms a candidate insertion: pickup before drop-off, every segment checked for seats, accessible positions, payload and cargo space.
  5. C03 recomputes every existing passenger and delivery deadline on that vehicle after the insertion (CAP-002); any accepted limit that would fail rejects the insertion.
  6. C03 checks energy and next-task limits, counting shared travel, stop dwell, repositioning, turnaround and replenishment once per vehicle (CAP-003).
  7. Among feasible candidates, ranking selects one without relaxing any hard constraint (BKG-010).
  8. C03 holds the complete resource bundle — vehicle, seats or cargo space, bay, charge and work slots as required — in one D2 transaction (CAP-004, BKG-016) and returns holdId with expiresAt; C02 makes the offer with hold expiry.
  9. The commitment becomes binding only after the commit is verified (P11 4.1).

Alternative flows

  • Insertion into a pooled route. The request joins an existing vehicle mission. The vehicle's route hours change once; the number of bookings on the route does not multiply them (CAP-011). Detailed shared-ride rules follow P29 22.2.
  • Pre-positioning. A vehicle may be committed to move empty towards expected demand; it is counted as committed, and its empty travel is part of its vehicle-hours.
  • Intercity transfer. A vehicle moving to a different operating area requires explicit travel and authority (CAP-015); without both, it is not supply in the destination area.

Exception flows

  • No feasible candidate. C03 returns a binding reason — the constraint that prevented feasibility — and an alternative where one exists (CAP-006). The request is kept in reporting as unmet demand (CAP-007).
  • Stale vehicle or site evidence. The affected vehicle or site is excluded from supply, and any capacity it held stays blocked; it is not re-offered until evidence is current (P08 1.2).
  • Resource revision changed during evaluation. The D2 transaction fails its revision check; C03 re-evaluates on the new snapshot rather than committing against old state (BKG-017).
  • Hold expires before acceptance. HELD moves to EXPIRED and the unused hold is released (BKG-023); the vehicle returns to Ready unless it holds other commitments.
  • Commit outcome unknown. The reservation moves to RECONCILING, occupancy stays blocked and the original intent is queried (BKG-026).

25.D.5 Fleet-state conservation

Every vehicle in N_total is, at any instant, in exactly one of five states, so N_total = N_ready + N_committed + N_service + N_replenishing + N_unavailable holds at every evaluation (CAP-009). The transitions are drawn in D25.2.

StateA vehicle is counted here whenIt is not counted here when
ReadyIt is assignable now: current evidence, no hold, no task outstanding, energy and tasks for the next departure verifiedIts state is stale or a hold remains
CommittedIt is held for a bundle or moving empty to pre-positionThe hold has expired (it returns to Ready)
In serviceIt is executing a mission: travelling to pickup or carrying passengers / cargoExecution is unknown — then occupancy stays blocked until physical clearance (BKG-038)
ReplenishingIt is queued at, or using, energy and turnaround resourcesRequired work is complete and release is verified
UnavailableIt has a fault, needs inspection or field recovery, or is held after MRMRELEASE_ELIGIBLE = V ∧ C ∧ A ∧ F has let C03 reassess availability (P18 11.3)

The conservation relation is a consistency check, not a planning result. If the five counts do not sum to N_total, a vehicle is either double-counted (typically counted as ready while still held) or lost (typically an unknown execution not attributed to any state); both are defects. A pooled route is one vehicle mission and moves one vehicle between states, regardless of the number of bookings on it.

25.D.6 Vehicle workload screen

For a planning interval, Σ_r vehicleHours_r ≤ available vehicle-hours in the same interval (CAP-010). The sum runs over distinct vehicle routes r, and each route's hours include empty travel, dwell and energy stops; available vehicle-hours are those of vehicles that are not unavailable over the interval and are within their service windows. Available hours are reported separately from scheduled fleet hours (CAP-054).

The screen is necessary, not sufficient. It can pass while individual pickups fail, because it ignores where and when vehicles are. Segment capacity and local service windows are therefore checked separately (CAP-012), and the spatial and peak-time checks below are required in addition.

25.D.7 Spatial and peak-time checks

  • Average capacity is not feasibility. A fleet that is sufficient over the day can still miss pickups in a burst; acceptance uses demand bursts and directional imbalance by zone (CAP-013).
  • Directional imbalance. When demand flows predominantly one way, vehicles accumulate at destinations; the cost of returning them appears as empty travel and must be in vehicle-hours.
  • Operational reserve. A reserve is held for faults and recovery and is not offered for new demand (CAP-014); its size is a planning decision tested by the degraded-operation scenarios of P27.
  • Response capacity. When remote or field response capacity is exhausted, new commitments are restricted even if vehicles are available (OPS-074).

25.D.8 Hub allocation

Each hub resource is allocated as time intervals per resource (CAP-016), using ResourceInterval entries with startUTC and endUTC as a half-open interval, so that one booking ending and the next starting at the same instant do not conflict. The resource mapping is shown in D25.3.

  1. Exclusive resources (parking bays, pickup space) admit no overlap.
  2. Pooled resources (site power, connectors, dispensers) admit concurrent use whose sum stays within capacity; pooled demand is summed against each limit (CAP-017).
  3. Work positions and staff (cleaning, inspection, qualified staff within opening hours) are allocated as intervals and checked for staff eligibility.
  4. Accessible capacity only. Capacity that is out of service, outside opening hours or not reachable for the vehicle type is not reservable (CAP-018).
  5. Queues and derating. Queue length at a resource and any outage derating are propagated into the ready times of the vehicles that depend on it (CAP-019); this is how a hub problem becomes a later t_ready,v and therefore a reachability failure.

A hub count alone does not specify throughput or coverage. Several hubs with few connectors can deliver less than a single hub with many; a hub far from demand adds empty travel to every cycle.

25.D.9 Rules and invariants

R25.1
A vehicle is a candidate only if t_ready,v + travelTime(v, origin, departure time) ≤ latestPickup (CAP-001).
R25.2
Every insertion recomputes all existing passenger and delivery deadlines; accepted limits stay binding (CAP-002, BKG-005).
R25.3
Shared travel, dwell, repositioning, turnaround and replenishment are counted once per vehicle (CAP-003).
R25.4
A commitment holds the complete resource bundle and is confirmed only after verified commit (CAP-004, CAP-005).
R25.5
An infeasible request returns a binding reason and is retained as unmet demand (CAP-006, CAP-007).
R25.6
Each vehicle is in exactly one fleet state; the five counts sum to N_total (CAP-009).
R25.7
Pooling never multiplies route hours by bookings (CAP-011).
R25.8
Stale vehicle or site state blocks the affected capacity; it is never counted as supply (P08 1.2).
R25.9
Only accessible hub capacity is reservable; queues and derating propagate into ready times (CAP-018, CAP-019).
R25.10
Alternatives are compared under the same demand trace; a hub count alone is not a throughput or coverage claim (CAP-020).

25.D.10 Data and state

ResourceInterval (D2)
intervalId, bundleId, resourceId, startUTC, endUTC, capacityType, quantity, unit, reservationRev, allocationState. capacityType distinguishes exclusive from pooled use; quantity and unit express pooled consumption.
Resource / Capability
resourceId, kind, capabilityRev, status, observedAt, capacity, constraints, quality. observedAt and quality decide whether the resource counts as accessible.
ResourceBundle (D2)
bundleId, bundleRev, state, expiresAt, policyVersion, inputSnapshotRef. inputSnapshotRef records which vehicle, resource and energy revisions the decision used, so a later reviewer can reproduce it.
Planning record
Zone / time interval, OD input, initial vehicle positions, hub resources, availability policy and service windows; versioned so that alternatives are compared on identical inputs.

25.D.11 Interfaces used

  • I03: Plan, Hold(snapshot), holdId / expiresAt and CommitBundle between C02 and C03.
  • I04: vehicle position, ready time, ETA and availability via C04.
  • I05: Read capability(site, window, minEnergy) and limits / capabilityRev / age from C05 / site EMS.
  • C09: AllocationCommitted from the D2 outbox and MissionObserved from the C04 outbox.

25.D.12 Failure handling and recovery

ConditionEffect on capacityRecovery
Vehicle state stale or link lostVehicle excluded from supply; its holds and occupancy remain blockedCurrent evidence; release predicate if it was held
Site energy capability staleCharge intervals at that site not offeredFresh capability with current capabilityRev
Connector or bay out of serviceRemoved from accessible capacity; dependent ready times recomputedResource status restored and observed
Queue growth at hubLater t_ready,v; some pickups become infeasible with binding reasonsQueue reduces; re-evaluation at the next planning interval
Vehicle fault in serviceMoves to unavailable; passengers re-planned via C02RELEASE_ELIGIBLE and reassessment by C03
Demand burst beyond reserveInfeasible requests rejected with reasons; unmet demand recordedService-mode decisions under P27 20.1

25.D.13 Observability and reporting

The observable outcomes of 18.3 are reported per planning interval and per zone: passenger and freight fulfillment; detour, delay and unmet requests; handling, queue and recovery load; and net contribution per vehicle-hour. Unmet demand is reported with its binding reasons, because the reason indicates the lever — vehicles, hub resources, energy or response capacity. The five fleet counts are reported over time, so that the share of the fleet that is replenishing or unavailable is visible next to the share that is ready. Measure definitions, denominators and exclusions follow P28 21.1; people counts are kept separate from booking counts (CAP-056).

25.D.14 Verification approach

  • Reachability and insertion. Requests at the edge of the pickup window, with t_ready,v affected by replenishment and queues; insertions that would break an existing passenger or delivery deadline must be rejected with a binding reason.
  • Conservation. At every step of a scenario, the five counts sum to N_total; injected unknown executions and expired holds must not create or lose vehicles.
  • Workload screen. Pooled routes with several bookings must contribute their route hours once.
  • Spatial and peak. Demand bursts and directional imbalance by zone, using repeatable demand traces or recorded seeds (CAP-059).
  • Hub limits. Overlapping bay requests, pooled power at its limit, staff outside opening hours and outage derating.
  • Alternatives. Fleet size, hub placement and service policy compared on the same demand trace, only after all required operating conditions pass (CAP-062); finite synthetic results are reported as a tested envelope (CAP-061).

25.D.15 Design rationale and alternatives considered

Per-request reachability instead of aggregate ratios. Fleet-to-demand ratios are easy to compute and easy to misread. Testing each request against the actual ready time and time-dependent travel time of each candidate catches the cases that ratios average away: the right number of vehicles in the wrong place or at the wrong time.

Conservation as an explicit check. A common class of capacity defect is a vehicle counted in two places, for example ready and still held. Making the five-state sum an invariant checked at every evaluation turns such defects into detectable failures.

Intervals per resource instead of hub-level capacity. A hub-level number cannot express that one connector is free while all bays are occupied. Interval allocation per resource, with exclusive and pooled rules, models the binding resource directly and lets queues and derating propagate.

Retaining unmet demand. Reporting only served requests makes a constrained system look reliable. Keeping rejected and unmet demand with reasons is necessary for honest comparison of alternatives.

25.D.16 Open points

  • Required fleet: minimum tested fleet meeting all service gates, determined by fleet sweep (TBD-046).
  • Infrastructure limits for node power, energy and footprint (TBD-014) and operating limits for hours, staffing and recovery (TBD-013) — G2 constraint register.
  • Ranking weights (TBD-032).
  • Freshness budgets for vehicle and site evidence (TBD-006).
  • Fuel / H2 replenishment capability and fuel-to-energy conversion for dispenser resources (TBD-036).
  • Shared-ride thresholds and operating authority (TBD-029).

26.DDetailed specification

This section specifies how a vehicle’s replenishment stop is planned, executed and closed so that the next departure is both on time and energy-sufficient. It defines the responsibilities of C03, C05, C04 and C02 in one hub cycle, the rules that bind the departure constraint, the electrical and fuel bounds and the site limits, the data each check reads, the handling of shortages and uncertain outcomes, and the evidence that verifies the design. It builds on the joint reservation model of P09–P11, the energy control loop of P12 5.1 and the capacity model of P25.

26.D.1 Purpose and scope

A vehicle can only serve its next commitment if the stop between two missions fits inside the duty cycle. The stop consumes finite, shared resources: a bay, a connector or dispenser, site power or fuel stock, qualified staff and work positions for cleaning and inspection. The purpose of this specification is to make the stop a planned, reserved and verified part of the vehicle cycle rather than an unmodelled gap between missions.

In scope: the five stages of 19.1 (arrive, queue, replenish, turnaround, release) at one hub; the electrical and fuel / hydrogen branches of 19.2 with their distinct units; the site-level limits that couple several vehicles at the same hub; detection, re-planning and verified release after a shortage (19.3); and acceptance evidence. Out of scope: the internal control of site equipment (plant protection remains local to the site equipment, ENE-021), the energy scheduler’s optimisation objective (TBD-033), market commitments (P12 5.1) and settlement of measured delivery (P12 5.2).

Two acceptance conditions are kept apart throughout: daily energy sufficiency (the hub and fleet can supply the energy the day’s missions need) and on-time departure (each individual vehicle leaves with enough energy at the committed time). A plan can satisfy the first and still fail the second, so each is evaluated and reported separately (CAP-024, ENE-036).

26.D.2 Actors and responsibilities

Actor / containerResponsibility in the replenishment cycleOwns
C03 Joint reservation authority (Appendix B C03)Reserves bay, connector or dispenser, staff and work slots as time intervals; evaluates the departure constraint; recalculates departure readiness on any shortage; holds affected assignments; decides release of the vehicle for the next departure.D2: ResourceBundle, ResourceInterval
C05 Energy / EMS adapters (Appendix B C05)Answers capability reads; schedules charging power within site limits; journals plan revisions over I05; reconciles equipment response from observed power, energy and meter quality; sends shortages back to C03.D4: plans, ACKs and market commitments (EnergyPlan)
C04 Fleet / vehicle adapter (Appendix B C04)Reports arrival time and observed energy as MissionObserved; obtains the current D1 permit before releasing the next mission.D3: command and status journal
C02 Booking / activities (Appendix B C02)Issues or withholds the dispatch permit; revises the ETA and notifies the service owner of an affected assignment.D1: bookingRev, terms, intent, saga, dispatch permit
C06 Operations (Appendix B C06)Owns exceptions that cannot be resolved automatically (unknown external effect, failed compensation, unrecoverable shortage) with an owner and deadline.D5 / D7 cases
Site EMS, charger, dispenserExecutes accepted setpoints within local protection; reports observed power, energy, meter quality and site alarms.Local protection and outage behaviour
Hub staffPerform cleaning, inspection and passenger / cargo handling as approved tasks and record the required evidence.Task evidence (evidenceRef)
Equipment workstreamValidates the equipment limits that C05 uses (ENE-022).Equipment limit values

26.D.3 Preconditions and inputs

  1. The vehicle’s ResourceBundle holds a ResourceInterval for every resource the stop uses: bay, connector or dispenser, staff and work slots (D26.1 precondition; CAP-016). Each interval is half-open (startUTC, endUTC) and carries capacityType: exclusive intervals must not overlap; pooled intervals sum to no more than capacity (BKG-017).
  2. C05 has received the mobility constraints for the bundle from C03: bundleId, arrival, departure, E_arrival, E_next_trip, E_reserve, bay / work / charge intervals, priority and accepted service promise (ENE-003).
  3. The capability of the site is available as a versioned input carrying capabilityRev, observedAt and quality (ENE-004). The resource snapshot and the energy capability are separate versioned inputs, not one shared revision (BKG-008).
  4. For the electrical branch an EnergyPlan exists in D4 with planId, planRev, bundleId, capabilityRev, validUntil and powerIntervals[] (ENE-013) and departureMinKWh for the next departure.
  5. For the fuel / hydrogen branch, the usable stock, dispenser flow and turnaround bounds are known (ENE-028). Control and observation of this branch is not carried by I05; it requires a separate capability (ENE-020, TBD-036).
  6. The next departure and every downstream delivery commitment of the vehicle are known from D1 / D2, so that t_departure and E_next_trip (or m_next_trip) can be evaluated.

26.D.4 Behaviour

Main flow. One vehicle cycle at a hub, as drawn in D26.1:

  1. C04 publishes MissionObserved with the arrival time and observed energy (or stock). C03 records t_arrival and the arrival quantity from the observation, not from the plan.
  2. C03 matches the arrival to the held bay and connector / dispenser intervals and to staff eligibility. If the held interval has not yet started, the waiting time is t_queue. Occupied connectors must stay within serviceable connectors at every interval (ENE-031).
  3. C03 reads the site capability through C05 (Read capability(site,window,minEnergy)) and receives limits, capabilityRev and age. Stale capability blocks the affected capacity and triggers re-planning (ENE-024; freshness budget TBD-006).
  4. C05 validates current limits, persists the I05 plan command and then sends it (ENE-014, ENE-015). The response is recorded as ACK, reject or unknown (ENE-016). The scheduled power at the site respects Σ P_charge,i(t) ≤ P_site,available(t) at every interval (ENE-030).
  5. During replenishment C05 receives observed power, energy and meter quality and publishes EnergyUpdated. It revises feasibility from these observations and from site alarms, including site derating (ENE-023).
  6. Turnaround tasks (passenger / cargo handling, cleaning, inspection as applicable) run in their reserved work slots. Only tasks approved to overlap may run in parallel with replenishment or with each other (CAP-022). Each task records its required evidence.
  7. C03 evaluates the release guard on observed values: the departure constraint t_arrival + t_queue + t_replenish + t_required_work ≤ t_departure (CAP-021) and the energy bound E_next_trip + E_reserve ≤ E_depart ≤ E_usable,max (ENE-026), or the mass bound for the fuel branch (ENE-027). It rechecks route energy and all next departure / delivery commitments (CAP-023).
  8. C03 releases the vehicle for the next departure; the bay and connector intervals are closed on observed clearance.
  9. C04 requests the current D1 permit before releasing the next mission (BKG-048). Only CONFIRMED + no pending cancel can issue a current dispatch permit (BKG-047); otherwise the vehicle stays blocked.

Alternative flows.

  1. Early arrival. The vehicle waits for its held interval; t_queue grows but the departure constraint may still hold. No interval is advanced unless C03 can hold the earlier interval without breaking another vehicle’s exclusive or pooled limit.
  2. Fuel / hydrogen branch. Steps 3–5 apply with mass instead of energy, through the separate fuel / H2 capability rather than I05 (ENE-020): m_depart = m_arrive + m_delivered − m_consumed, bounded by dispenser flow and usable stock; site fuel stock remains non-negative after deliveries and withdrawals (ENE-033). No conversion between kg and kWh is applied unless an explicit model exists (ENE-029).
  3. Several resources at one hub. A hub can contain several resources; C03 may assign any serviceable connector or dispenser of the required kind, provided the assignment is a new held interval in the bundle and not an untracked substitution.
  4. No replenishment needed. If observed arrival energy already satisfies the energy bound for the next trip, the replenish stage is skipped; turnaround and the departure constraint still apply.

Exception flows. Shortage propagation follows 19.3 and D26.2:

  1. C05 detects power derating, site outage, low stock or supply delay, or C03 detects queue growth, a delayed arrival, or stale capability or meter data. All are treated as the same input to re-planning (CAP-025); an infeasible energy schedule is sent back to C03 (ENE-005).
  2. C03 recalculates departure readiness for every vehicle whose bundle uses the affected resource, not only the vehicle that triggered the signal.
  3. If a feasible alternative site or vehicle exists, C03 holds the replacement before it retires the old capacity; the swap applies only to unstarted allocations, and started or unknown missions retain occupancy until physical clearance (CAP-026, BKG-038). The change is published as AllocationCommitted.
  4. Otherwise C03 holds the affected assignments. C02 revises the ETA and notifies the service owner (CAP-027) and publishes BookingChanged via the outbox.
  5. If an I05 response is unknown, C05 queries the status of the same planId until the outcome is resolved or escalated (ENE-017); C03 keeps the PENDING occupancy blocked and the quote TTL does not release it (ENE-018).
  6. Capacity returns to the plan only after the actual delivered quantity is observed, inspection and required work are complete and current resource revisions are confirmed (CAP-028, ENE-034).

26.D.5 Rules and invariants

R26.1
Every resource used by the stop is a ResourceInterval in the vehicle’s ResourceBundle; no stage starts on an unreserved resource (CAP-016, CAP-004).
R26.2
The departure constraint holds on observed times before release; required work includes passenger / cargo handling, cleaning and inspection as applicable (CAP-021).
R26.3
Only approved tasks overlap. A task that is not approved to overlap is added sequentially to t_required_work (CAP-022).
R26.4
Electrical release requires E_next_trip + E_reserve ≤ E_depart ≤ E_usable,max on observed values, with E_depart from E_arrive + η_ch ∫ P_AC(t) dt − E_aux using charger / battery limits and charging efficiency (ENE-025, ENE-026). The upper bound is binding in planning: a plan may not count energy above E_usable,max towards the next trip.
R26.5
Fuel / hydrogen release requires m_next_trip + m_reserve ≤ m_depart ≤ m_usable,max; usable stock, dispenser flow and turnaround are bounded; fuel stock remains non-negative (ENE-027, ENE-028, ENE-033).
R26.6
Electrical quantities use kW, hours and kWh; fuel quantities use kg, kg/min and minutes. Fuel-to-energy conversion requires an explicit model (ENE-029, ASM-018).
R26.7
At every time interval Σ P_charge,i(t) ≤ P_site,available(t) and occupied connectors ≤ serviceable connectors (ENE-030, ENE-031). P_site,available reflects building load, generation, storage and connection limits at the same boundary as the AC bus balance (ENE-032, ENE-008).
R26.8
An I05 plan ACK is not delivered energy; release and capacity return use the observed delivered quantity (ENE-019, ENE-034, ASM-019).
R26.9
Stale capability or meter data blocks the affected capacity and triggers re-planning; missing data is never defaulted to the planned value (ENE-024).
R26.10
Replacement capacity is held before old capacity is retired; started or unknown allocations keep occupancy until physical clearance (BKG-038, BKG-039).
R26.11
Release for the next departure does not itself authorise motion: the next mission still requires the current D1 permit (BKG-048).
R26.12
Daily energy sufficiency and on-time departure are separate acceptance conditions; reserve violations and unmet trips are reported even when aggregate daily energy balances (CAP-024, ENE-036).

26.D.6 Data and state

The cycle uses existing entities only. The table maps each term of the departure constraint and the energy bounds to the record that supplies it at planning time and at release.

TermPlanning sourceRelease source (observed)
t_arrivalMission plan of the inbound bundleMissionObserved arrival time (C04)
t_queueStart of the held bay / connector ResourceIntervalObserved start of occupancy
t_replenishCharge interval and EnergyPlan powerIntervals[]; dispenser intervalEnergyUpdated (observed power / energy / meter quality)
t_required_workWork-slot intervals of the approved tasksTask completion with evidenceRef
t_departureNext bundle departure / committed pickupUnchanged unless re-planned (BookingChanged)
E_arrive / m_arriveE_arrival from C03 mobility constraintsObserved energy (or stock) on arrival
E_next_trip, E_reserveC03 mobility constraints to C05Rechecked against the current route revision
E_depart / m_departComputed from the planComputed from observed delivery, never from ACK
P_site,availableCapability with capabilityRev, observedAt and qualityObserved site capability and alarms

State is carried by existing models: allocationState of each ResourceInterval in D2, the booking and bundle states of P09 2.3 (HELD, COMMIT_PENDING, CONFIRMED, RECONCILING), the I05 plan outcome (ACK / reject / unknown) and acceptedRev and executionEvidence of the EnergyPlan in D4, and the fleet-count category N_replenishing of P25 18.2. A vehicle in the queue or replenish stage counts in N_replenishing (queue / energy); a vehicle held for a fault or inspection counts in N_unavailable. In neither case is it counted as ready before release, even if its energy bound already holds, because required work may still be open. No additional state is introduced for the five stages; they are views over the intervals and observations above.

Metered actuals of the delivered energy flow to C07 over I08 (meterPointId, interval, sourceRev, quantity, unit, contractRev) for settlement (ENE-037). Availability kW and delivered kWh remain distinct quantities (ENE-052).

26.D.7 Interfaces used

Interface / eventUse in this chapter
I03 Joint reservationHold and atomic replacement of bay, charge and work slots; binding reason when infeasible.
I04 Mission / executionArrival and observed energy; release of the next mission after the D1 permit.
I05 Energy capability and plan journalCapability read, plan revision, ACK / reject / unknown, status query; equipment feedback. Electrical scope only.
I08 Metered actualsMeasured delivery for settlement and for acceptance evidence.
C09 Event backboneMissionObserved, EnergyUpdated, AllocationCommitted, BookingChanged; at-least-once delivery with an idempotent inbox and per-aggregate revision.

Because C09 is at-least-once, a repeated EnergyUpdated must not increase E_depart twice: consumers apply an observation only once per aggregate revision and fetch a gap rather than infer missing values.

26.D.8 Failure handling and recovery

FailureDetectionHandlingRecovery condition
Power derating / site outageSite alarms, observed power below plan (C05)C05 revises feasibility; shortage to C03; departure readiness recalculated for all affected bundlesObserved capability restored with a current capabilityRev
Low stock / supply delayStock observation, delivery statusHold assignments that depend on the stock; alternative site / vehicle if feasibleStock observed non-negative after planned withdrawals
Queue growth / delayed arrivalMissionObserved later than plan; occupancy of serviceable connectorsRecompute t_queue for subsequent vehicles; re-plan intervalsDeparture constraint holds for every affected vehicle
Stale capability or meter dataAge or quality outside the freshness budget (TBD-006)Block the affected capacity; trigger re-planning (ENE-024)Fresh observation with acceptable quality
Unknown I05 responseNo ACK / reject within the journalQuery the same planId; keep PENDING occupancy blocked; escalate to an owned case if unresolvedOutcome resolved by query
Delivered quantity below planEnergyUpdated / I08 below the planRelease guard fails; extend or re-plan the interval, or hold the next assignmentEnergy or mass bound holds on observed values
Required work incompleteMissing task evidenceNo release; t_required_work re-estimated; ETA revised if the departure constraint failsEvidence recorded for every required task
Rejected / conflicting planI05 rejectCompensation starts (release old / undo new as required); failed compensation stays owned (BKG-044, BKG-045)Reconciled outcome recorded

Recovery never releases capacity on an inference. A connector reported serviceable again is reusable only after its current revision is confirmed; a vehicle whose replenishment outcome is unknown keeps its interval occupied until physical clearance.

26.D.9 Security, privacy and audit

  • Plans, ACKs and market commitments are recorded in D4 (ENE-006); each I05 command is persisted before it is sent, so every setpoint sent to a site can be traced to a plan revision and a capability snapshot.
  • Keys include tenant scope; a bundle, plan or site reference is validated within that scope (ASM-009).
  • C05 never overrides site protection: plant protection, local protection and outage behaviour remain at the site (ENE-021). A setpoint is a request within limits, not a command that bypasses equipment limits.
  • Household sites (P12 5.1) expose household load and connection limits; only the limits needed for P_site,available are used in scheduling, and the household’s self-use is not part of the service electricity term (ENE-045).
  • Measured delivery is not overwritten; corrections are correction entries linked to the original record (ENE-040).

26.D.10 Observability and operations

Operations need to see, per hub and interval: occupied versus serviceable connectors, scheduled versus available site power, queue duration per vehicle, vehicles held for a shortage, capability age and meter quality, and the margin of each vehicle against its departure constraint and energy bound. Each re-planning event is traceable from its trigger (EnergyUpdated or MissionObserved) through the AllocationCommitted and BookingChanged it produced. Reserve violations and missed departures are reported per vehicle, alongside the daily energy balance, so that a balanced day does not hide individual failures.

26.D.11 Verification approach

  1. Run the four acceptance tests of 19.3 against the constraint each exercises (D26.3), recording arrival / departure energy, measured delivery, queue duration, site-limit trace and missed departures (ENE-035).
  2. Check the site-limit trace interval by interval, not as an aggregate: every interval must satisfy R26.7.
  3. Inject an unknown I05 response and confirm that occupancy stays blocked, the same planId is queried and no capacity is released on the quote TTL (ENE-018; fault pattern of P24 17.2).
  4. Feed an ACK without delivery and confirm the release guard fails (R26.8).
  5. Feed stale capability and meter data and confirm the affected capacity is blocked (R26.9).
  6. Construct a day whose aggregate energy balances but in which one vehicle misses its reserve; confirm it is reported as a reserve violation (R26.12).
  7. Repeat the electrical cases on the fuel branch with mass units and confirm no implicit unit conversion occurs (R26.6).

These are planned tests; the results become G3 evidence only when run (TBD-052, ASM-030).

26.D.12 Design rationale and alternatives considered

Reserve the stop as intervals
Treating replenishment as an unavailability block on the vehicle is simpler but hides contention between vehicles for the same connector, staff and site power. Holding each resource as an interval lets C03 apply the same exclusive / pooled checks it uses for seats and bays, and makes queue growth visible before it becomes a missed departure.
Observed values for release
A plan ACK only confirms that the site accepted a request. Derating, connector faults or a short session can leave the vehicle below its bound. Releasing on observed delivery costs latency at release but prevents a vehicle departing on energy that was never delivered.
Per-interval site limit
A daily energy budget can be met while the site power limit is exceeded in a peak interval. The limit is therefore stated at every time interval and at the same boundary as the AC bus balance of P12 5.1.
Distinct units
A single energy unit for both branches would require a conversion whose assumptions (efficiency, fuel quality) are not modelled. Keeping kg and kWh apart until an explicit model exists avoids a silent error in the release guard.
Two acceptance conditions
Energy sufficiency answers whether the hub can supply the fleet; on-time departure answers whether the service promise is kept. Merging them would let a surplus at one hour mask a shortfall at another.

26.D.13 Open points

  • Freshness budgets for capability and meter data (TBD-006, decided at G2).
  • Node power / energy / footprint limits of each hub (TBD-014) and hours / staffing / recovery limits (TBD-013), both in the G2 constraint register.
  • Fuel / H2 replenishment capability and the explicit fuel-to-energy conversion model (TBD-036), including how dispensers are represented as resources.
  • C05 scheduler objective (TBD-033) and the optional C05 optimisation outside the MVP (TBD-022).
  • I05 protocol (TBD-003) and district CEMS / GTFC limits (TBD-037).
